Never redirect to a client-supplied URL without validation: accept only paths that start with a single slash, and reject // and backslashes, because browsers treat /\evil.example like //evil.example, a protocol-relative URL to another host.
sections.title: Pick the redirect status by what must survive

sections.body: Extend the route-table test from the route-groups lesson: for every entry in r.Routes(), send the common methods that are not registered and assert 405, the exact Allow value and a JSON Content-Type. Add HEAD for every GET route you expect monitors to probe, an unknown path, a trailing-slash variant, each redirect's status and Location, and a list of hostile next values including //host, /\host and https://host.
sections.title: Test the misses as carefully as the hits

readings.takeaway: Turn on HandleMethodNotAllowed, answer misses through NoRoute and NoMethod in your normal error format, register HEAD explicitly where it is probed, and use 303, 307 or 308 whenever the method or body must survive a redirect.
readings.title: 404, 405 and redirects in Gin: answer misses in your own format and pick redirect codes by what must survive
wrongAnswers: Yes; Gin runs the GET handler and drops the body
Yes, but only when HandleMethodNotAllowed is enabled

cautions: Routes registered outside the group, or before Use, are public.
Stateless HMAC tokens cannot be revoked before expiry without extra state.
designGuide.cost: One HMAC per request is cheap; the real cost is key management: rotation, storage in a secret manager and a revocation story.
strengths: One verification point covers every route in the group.
Handlers receive a typed principal instead of raw headers.

readings.hint: Would sending the same request again with a freshly issued copy of this token change the outcome?
readings.introduction: Authentication middleware turns an Authorization header into one of two outcomes before any handler runs: a verified principal, or a refusal the client can act on. The bugs live at the edges of that job: a route registered outside the protected group, a MAC compared with ==, a 403 where the client needed a 401, or a debug log that quietly archives every credential it sees.
readings.nuance: 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid, so a retry with good ones may succeed. This token verified, so the refusal is about permission, which RFC 6750 signals with 403 and insufficient_scope.
readings.objective: Write middleware that verifies an HMAC-signed bearer token, stores a typed principal and answers 401 or 403 for the right reasons.
readings.question: A caller sends a valid, unexpired bearer token that lacks the notes:admin scope to an admin-only route. What should the middleware answer?
readings.reviewAnswer: 403 with error="insufficient_scope"

sections.body: Authentication answers who is calling; authorization answers whether that caller may do this. Keep them in separate middleware so each has one reason to refuse. A 401 Unauthorized means the request carried no usable credentials and a retry with valid ones may succeed; RFC 9110 requires a WWW-Authenticate header on every 401 so the client learns which scheme to use. A 403 Forbidden means the server knows exactly who is calling and the answer is still no, so logging in again will not help. RFC 6750 refines this for bearer tokens: a request with no token gets a bare challenge, an invalid or expired token gets error="invalid_token", and a valid token without the needed scope gets 403 with error="insufficient_scope". Neither middleware decides whether note 7 belongs to user-42. That ownership check needs the stored data, so it belongs to the use case, which receives the principal as an argument.
sections.title: Decide what the middleware owns

sections.body: An opaque token is a string the client stores and sends back but never interprets. Here it is base64url(subject|scopes|expiry) followed by a dot and an HMAC-SHA256 tag over those bytes, keyed with a server secret. The verifier recomputes the tag and compares it with hmac.Equal, whose running time does not depend on where the first differing byte is; == on strings or bytes.Equal may stop early and leak how much of a guess was right. Only a payload with a valid tag is parsed, and expiry is checked against an injected clock so tests never sleep. The program forges an admin token by swapping the payload while keeping a real tag, and replays an expired one.
sections.title: Verify the MAC first, then trust the payload
sections.walkthrough: Verify splits at the first dot, decodes both halves and recomputes the tag before parsing anything, so the forged admin payload fails as a bad signature without its scopes ever being read. authenticate compares the scheme with strings.EqualFold because auth schemes are case-insensitive, which is why the lowercase bearer request succeeds. Each refusal sets WWW-Authenticate before AbortWithStatusJSON writes the response, and the rejection log line carries the route and a reason code but no token. c.Set stores the Principal under the unexported principalKey type, and principalFrom is the only reader, so handlers get a typed value instead of re-parsing headers. requireScope runs inside the admin group, after authenticate, and answers 403 with insufficient_scope. The JSON log handler drops the time attribute so the output is stable.

sections.body: The route group is the policy boundary: anything registered on api passes through authenticate, anything registered on r is public, whether or not that was intended. Gin copies a group's middleware into each route's handler chain at registration time, so calling api.Use(authenticate) after a route was added does not protect that earlier route; it keeps answering 200 to anonymous callers. Pass middleware to Group or call Use before registering routes, and make the gap testable. r.Routes() lists every registered method and path, which lets one test send an anonymous request to each route outside a short public allow-list and fail when any of them answers something other than 401.
sections.title: Public and protected routes are a wiring decision
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is a go test that runs in your own project, next to newRouter. testVerifier is a helper that builds a Verifier with a fixed test key and clock, and slog.DiscardHandler keeps the rejection logs out of the test output. A path such as /api/admin/notes/:id is sent literally, which still matches the parameterized route with id set to ":id". New routes are covered automatically, so a forgotten group fails CI instead of production.

sections.body: A bearer token is a password with an expiry date: anyone who copies it from a log file can replay it until then. Log a stable reason code such as bad signature or expired, never the header value, and keep the public response generic so clients cannot tell a forged token from an expired one. Do not accept tokens in query strings: gin.Logger records the path together with the raw query unless SkipQueryString is set, and proxies and browser history keep URLs too. Gin's Recovery middleware in debug mode dumps the request headers with only Authorization masked, so a Cookie header is printed as is. Routing every log through one redaction step, covered in the request-logging lesson, is safer than auditing each call site.
sections.title: Keep credentials out of logs, URLs and error bodies

sections.body: This verifier is a model; it shows the order of checks, not a complete token system. Real deployments rotate keys, so prefix tokens with a key ID and accept the previous key for one token lifetime. A stateless HMAC token cannot be revoked before it expires, so keep lifetimes short or, when instant logout matters, issue random tokens and store their SHA-256 hash in a session table you can delete from, at the cost of one lookup per request. Load keys of at least 32 random bytes from a secret manager and use a separate key per purpose. The pipe separator only works because the issuer controls the subject; use a structured encoding for anything richer, or a vetted JWT or PASETO library that pins the algorithm. Test missing, malformed, forged, expired, wrong-scope and lowercase-scheme tokens as separate cases, and assert on headers and body as well as on the status.
sections.title: What a production verifier adds

readings.takeaway: Authenticate at the group boundary, compare MACs with hmac.Equal before parsing anything, store a typed principal under an unexported key, answer 401 with WWW-Authenticate for bad credentials and 403 for missing permission, and never log the token.
readings.title: Bearer authentication in Gin: verify once at the group boundary, hand handlers a typed principal
wrongAnswers: 401 with error="invalid_token" so the client refreshes
400, because the request asked for the wrong scope

cautions: CORS does not stop non-browser clients or CSRF form posts.
Group-scoped CORS middleware never sees unmatched OPTIONS preflights.
designGuide.cost: A small middleware and a list of origins to maintain per environment; the risk is in the configuration, so test it like code.
strengths: Exact origins and validated config make the policy reviewable.
Engine-level middleware handles preflights without OPTIONS routes.

readings.hint: Think about what * would mean for the cookies of every signed-in user on every website.
readings.introduction: CORS is the protocol a server uses to tell a browser which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it never tightens it. Done carelessly it either breaks a legitimate front end or lets any website read a signed-in user's data. Done correctly it is still not authentication, authorization or CSRF protection, and the server has to keep enforcing those on its own.
readings.nuance: Browsers refuse * when credentials are included, so the server must echo one allow-listed origin and add Vary: Origin. Reflecting any origin instead would expose authenticated data to every site.
readings.objective: Implement CORS middleware that answers preflights, echoes only allow-listed origins, sets Vary correctly and is never mistaken for access control.
readings.question: Can a server answer a credentialed request with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and still let the page read the response?
readings.reviewAnswer: Rejected: credentialed requests need an exact origin

sections.body: Simple requests, such as a GET or a form POST with no custom headers, are sent straight to the server with an Origin header; afterwards the browser checks Access-Control-Allow-Origin to decide whether page script may read the answer. Anything else, such as PUT, DELETE, a JSON content type or an Authorization header, first triggers a preflight: an OPTIONS request carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The browser sends the real request only if the preflight response approves that origin, method and set of headers. For a simple request the handler has already run by the time the browser decides, so CORS controls who may read a response, not who may send a request. Requests made with credentials, meaning cookies or fetch with credentials: "include", additionally need Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an explicit origin.
sections.title: What the browser asks and what the server decides

sections.body: The middleware runs engine-wide. It adds Vary: Origin to every response, echoes an allow-listed origin exactly, and terminates preflights itself with 204 so no handler runs. The constructor validates configuration, so the dangerous combinations fail at startup instead of in a browser console. Five requests show an approved preflight, a refused one, a credentialed GET, a GET from an unknown origin and a GET with no Origin at all.
sections.title: An allow-list middleware that answers preflights
sections.walkthrough: newCORS rejects "*" combined with credentials and the "null" origin before any request is served. Inside the middleware, Header().Add appends to Vary rather than overwriting a value another layer set. A preflight is an OPTIONS request that carries Access-Control-Request-Method; the requested method and every requested header are checked against the configured lists, lowercased because header names are case-insensitive, and the allowed preflight ends with AbortWithStatus(204). No OPTIONS route is registered, yet the preflight still reaches the middleware because r.Use also attaches it to Gin's 404 chain. The evil.example preflight is refused with 403. Its simple GET still gets 200 and the JSON body, only without CORS headers.

sections.body: When the response echoes the caller's origin, its headers depend on the Origin request header, and caches must know that. Without Vary: Origin, a shared cache or the browser's own HTTP cache can store the copy made for app.example.com and replay it to another origin, or store the copy made for a request with no Origin and replay it to a cross-origin fetch, which then fails with an error that looks random. So add Vary: Origin to every response from CORS-enabled routes, including refusals and requests without an Origin header. The wildcard means any origin may read, and browsers reject it for credentialed requests. The tempting workaround, reflecting whatever Origin arrives while also sending Allow-Credentials: true, is worse than the wildcard: it lets every website read the user's authenticated data. Never allow-list the null origin either, because sandboxed iframes and local files send it and an attacker can produce it on purpose. Compare whole origins exactly; strings.HasSuffix(origin, "example.com") also accepts https://evilexample.com.
sections.title: Vary: Origin and the wildcard rule

sections.body: Gin runs a group's middleware only for routes that matched. A preflight for /api/notes matches nothing unless an OPTIONS route exists, so CORS middleware attached to the api group never sees it and Gin answers 404, or 405 when HandleMethodNotAllowed is enabled. Middleware registered with Engine.Use is also part of the 404 and 405 handler chains, which is why the program registers CORS there. Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache an approved preflight. Without it the default is 5 seconds, and browsers cap whatever you send: Firefox at 24 hours, current Chromium at 2 hours. Ten minutes removes most preflight round trips while still letting a configuration change take effect quickly. Check Access-Control-Request-Headers against a list instead of echoing it back, so a front end cannot quietly start sending headers nobody has reviewed. The same applies to Access-Control-Expose-Headers: list response headers such as ETag explicitly if page script needs to read them.
sections.title: Preflight routing and max-age in Gin

sections.body: The 200 for https://evil.example in the output is the key point: the handler ran and produced data, and only the browser declined to hand it to the page. curl, server-side scripts and attack tools ignore CORS, so every endpoint must still authenticate and authorize each request itself. CORS also does not stop cross-site request forgery. A form POST, or a simple fetch that carries cookies, is sent cross-origin without a preflight and the server performs the side effect; the attacker only loses the ability to read the reply. Cookie-authenticated APIs therefore need CSRF defenses: SameSite cookies, a synchronizer or double-submit token, or rejecting state-changing requests whose Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site header names another site. Bearer tokens sent in an Authorization header are not attached by the browser automatically, which is why they avoid classic CSRF. When reviewing a CORS change, test an approved and a refused preflight, a disallowed method and header, a credentialed request, the presence of Vary on every response and the configuration checks.
sections.title: What CORS does not protect

readings.takeaway: CORS relaxes the browser's read barrier for an exact list of origins: answer preflights at the engine level, echo the origin together with Vary: Origin, never pair * or a reflected origin with credentials, and keep authentication and CSRF defenses on the server.
readings.title: CORS by hand in Gin: an exact origin allow-list, real preflights and Vary: Origin
wrongAnswers: Yes, * covers every origin, credentialed or not
Yes, as long as Allow-Credentials: true is also sent

cautions: An IP key is only as good as the trusted-proxy configuration.
In-process limits multiply by the number of replicas.
designGuide.cost: One small struct per active client and a mutex on the map; a global limit additionally costs a shared store and a round trip per request.
strengths: Per-identity buckets isolate noisy clients from everyone else.
Explicit times make every limiter decision unit-testable.

readings.hint: ReserveN has already updated the bucket as if the request would run later.
readings.introduction: A rate limiter protects shared capacity from one noisy client. Three decisions matter more than the algorithm: what identifies a client, how much memory the limiter may use, and what a refused client is told. Choose the key badly and an attacker gets a fresh bucket on every request. Forget the memory bound and the limiter becomes the leak it was meant to prevent.
readings.nuance: A reservation with a delay borrows a token from the future. If the request is dropped instead of delayed, CancelAt returns that token, so the client is not charged for work that never happened.
readings.objective: Limit each client with golang.org/x/time/rate, pick a key clients cannot forge, bound the limiter map and refuse with 429 and Retry-After.
readings.question: The middleware calls ReserveN, sees a positive delay and answers 429 without waiting. Why should it call CancelAt on the reservation?
readings.reviewAnswer: So the refused request does not consume a future token

sections.body: rate.NewLimiter(r, b) models a bucket that holds up to b tokens and refills at r tokens per second; each request takes one. The burst b absorbs short spikes, and r is the sustained rate. A Limiter is safe for concurrent use, but a map of limiters is not, so the store needs its own mutex. The methods differ in what happens when the bucket is empty. Allow reports false and nothing else. Wait blocks until a token arrives, which in an HTTP handler means holding a goroutine and a connection open for a client you meant to slow down. Reserve says how long until a token will be available, which is exactly the number Retry-After needs. AllowN and ReserveN take an explicit time.Time, so a test can drive the limiter with a fake clock instead of sleeping.
sections.title: Token buckets and the x/time/rate API

sections.body: The program allows one request per second with a burst of two and keeps at most three buckets. A stand-in for the auth middleware sets the subject. Anonymous callers are keyed by ClientIP, which only means something because the engine trusts exactly one proxy address. A fake clock drives every decision, so the output never depends on how fast the machine is.
sections.title: Key by identity, bound the store, refuse with Retry-After
sections.walkthrough: get moves an existing bucket to the front of the LRU list, or creates a new one and evicts the back entry when the store is full. rateLimit calls ReserveN at the fake time. A positive delay means the bucket is empty, so the middleware calls CancelAt: otherwise the refused request would still hold a future token and the client would be charged twice. The delay is then rounded up to whole seconds for Retry-After. The third request from user-17 at t=0 is refused with Retry-After=1. The direct peer 203.0.113.9 is not a trusted proxy, so ClientIP ignores its forged X-Forwarded-For values and all three requests share one bucket. At t=1s user-17 has a token again; without the CancelAt call this request would also be refused, because the dropped reservation would still hold that token. The fourth key evicts the least recently used bucket, ip:198.51.100.7.

sections.body: The key decides who shares a bucket. A verified subject is the best key: it survives IP changes and maps to a quota a customer can understand, so authenticate before you limit and keep that check cheap. For anonymous endpoints such as login, sign-up and public search, the client address is the only signal, and it is only as trustworthy as your proxy configuration. With SetTrustedProxies covering exactly your load balancer, ClientIP returns the forwarded address. If every peer is trusted, a client can write any address into X-Forwarded-For and get a new bucket each time, as the trusted-proxies lesson shows. Even a correct address key is coarse. Many users behind one carrier NAT or office gateway share an address, and an IPv6 client can rotate through the prefix it was assigned, often a /64, so consider keying IPv6 by prefix. A login endpoint usually needs two limits: per account to slow password guessing, and per address to slow credential stuffing across many accounts.
sections.title: Choose a key clients cannot forge

sections.body: Every new key allocates a limiter, so an unbounded map lets anyone who can vary the key grow your heap without limit. The LRU list caps the store with constant-time updates. Eviction has a price: an evicted client comes back with a full bucket, so heavy key churn makes the limit looser, never stricter. That is the right direction to fail for availability, but it means the cap must comfortably exceed the number of clients active at once. A bucket that has been idle for burst divided by rate seconds has refilled completely and behaves exactly like a new one, so dropping those entries loses nothing; a periodic sweep of idle entries keeps the LRU from pushing out active clients. The store also lives in one process. Behind a round-robin balancer, N replicas give each client roughly N times the configured rate. A global quota needs shared state, for example Redis updated atomically, at the cost of a network round trip per request.
sections.title: Bound the map and know what eviction costs

sections.body: Answer 429 Too Many Requests, defined in RFC 6585, with Retry-After in whole seconds, rounded up, because a client that retries early is simply refused again. RFC 9110 allows either a number of seconds or an HTTP date; seconds avoid clock-skew problems. Keep the refusal cheap: the goal is to shed work, so do not run the handler, and at high volume count refusals per route instead of writing a full log line for each one. Well-behaved clients add jitter to their retries so they do not return in lockstep. A per-client limit is not overload protection. When the whole service is saturated, a global concurrency limit that answers 503 protects capacity even though every client is within its own quota. Test a burst followed by a refusal, a refill after the advertised Retry-After, independent buckets, forged forwarding headers, eviction at the cap, and concurrent requests under the race detector.
sections.title: What a refused client should see

readings.takeaway: Key buckets by a verified identity, or by ClientIP only with trusted proxies configured. Bound the map and accept that eviction loosens limits, drive the limiter with explicit times, and refuse with 429 and a rounded-up Retry-After after canceling the unused reservation.
readings.title: Rate limiting in Gin: a token bucket per identity, a bounded map and an honest Retry-After
wrongAnswers: CancelAt closes the limiter so the map can evict it
Without CancelAt the 429 response is never written

cautions: ReplaceAttr cannot see inside maps such as a logged http.Header.
Recovery registered outside the logger hides panicking requests.
designGuide.cost: One JSON line per request plus the storage behind it; sample or drop health probes when volume matters.
strengths: One request ID correlates logs, responses and support tickets.
Route templates keep log fields low-cardinality and free of secrets.

readings.hint: Count how many distinct values the field would hold after a million requests for different notes.
readings.introduction: An access log is what you search during an incident. It is only useful if every line carries the same small set of fields, if one request can be followed across services by an ID, and if the log never becomes a second copy of your users' credentials. Gin's built-in Logger prints raw paths with query strings as text, so production services usually replace it with middleware built on log/slog.
readings.nuance: FullPath has one value per registered route and never contains IDs or query strings, so it can be grouped and alerted on without leaking tokens or personal data.
readings.objective: Add request-ID middleware and a structured slog access log that records low-cardinality routes, redacts credentials and can be tested byte for byte.
readings.question: Which value should a Gin access log record as the request path to keep the log searchable and safe?
readings.reviewAnswer: c.FullPath(), the route template such as /notes/:id

sections.body: A request ID ties together the access line, application logs, downstream calls and the screenshot in a customer's bug report. If an edge proxy or calling service already assigned X-Request-ID, reuse it so the trail stays continuous; otherwise generate one. The incoming header is still client input. It can be very long, contain newlines that forge extra lines in text logs, or be chosen to collide with someone else's trail. Accept only a short value from a conservative alphabet and replace anything else. In production, crypto/rand.Text returns 26 base32 characters with at least 128 bits of randomness, enough that collisions are not a concern. Echo the ID in the response header so a client can quote it in a support ticket. If public clients can reach the service directly, consider always generating your own ID and logging the incoming one as a separate field.
sections.title: Accept a request ID only when it is well formed

sections.body: The chain is requestID, then accessLog, then recovery. The ID exists before anything logs, and the access log wraps everything after it, so it sees the final status even when a handler panics. Four requests cover a valid incoming ID with a token in the query string, a malicious ID, an unmatched path and a panic. The JSON handler uses test options that make the output stable.
sections.title: Request ID, access log and recovery in one chain
sections.walkthrough: requestID validates the incoming header, falls back to the injected generator, and stores the ID both in Gin's keys and in the request context, so code that only receives a context.Context can find it. accessLog calls c.Next first; after it returns, c.FullPath and c.Writer.Status are final. The first raw URL contained ?token=leaked, yet the line records only /notes/:id. The second ID contained a newline and was replaced with gen-000001. /admin.php matched no route, so FullPath is empty and the line says unmatched. The panic is caught by recovery, logged with the same request ID and turned into a 500, and the access log still records it. redact prints every authorization value as [REDACTED]; stableForTest also drops the time and pins latency to 0 so the output can be compared exactly.

sections.body: c.FullPath returns the registered pattern, such as /notes/:id. That keeps the field low-cardinality: you can group, count and alert per route, and the log index does not gain a new value for every note ID. Raw URLs also carry data that should not be stored, such as personal identifiers, email addresses in paths and tokens in query strings. Gin's Logger appends the raw query unless SkipQueryString is set. Unmatched requests are mostly scanners, and logging them under one unmatched value keeps them countable without flooding the index. When you need the concrete resource, log the validated parameter on purpose, for example as a note_id field. Order matters too. If Recovery is registered before the logger, a panic unwinds through the logger before its line is written, and the request you most need to see disappears from the access log.
sections.title: Log the route template, not the URL

sections.body: Redaction in HandlerOptions.ReplaceAttr applies to every record the logger writes, not only to the call sites a careful author remembered. ReplaceAttr runs for each non-group attribute, including attributes nested in groups, whose names it receives in the groups argument, and returning a zero Attr drops the attribute. It has a limit: it sees attributes, not the inside of values. slog.Any("headers", req.Header) is a single attribute whose value is a map, so a key-based ReplaceAttr never sees the Authorization entry inside it. Log an explicit allow-list of headers instead, or wrap secrets in a type whose LogValue method returns a redacted value. The test options call redact rather than replacing it, so tests run the same redaction code as production.
sections.title: Put redaction in the handler options
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the production wiring and runs in your own service. crypto/rand.Text already has the func() string shape that requestID expects. Time and latency stay real, and only redact remains in ReplaceAttr. Writing JSON to stdout lets the platform's log collector ship lines without the process managing files or rotation.

sections.body: Handlers should log through the request context with logger.InfoContext(ctx, ...). The stock JSON handler ignores context values, so either wrap it with a handler that copies request_id from the context into each record, or store logger.With("request_id", id) in the context. Forward X-Request-ID on outbound HTTP calls, plus traceparent if you use OpenTelemetry tracing. Log 5xx at Error and 4xx at Info: client errors are not server incidents, and alerting on them pages someone for every scanner. Health probes usually do not need a line each. Treat the log format as a contract and test it: decode each line as JSON and assert the fields, check that a known secret string never appears in the captured output, check that invalid IDs are replaced, and check that a panic still produces an access line.
sections.title: Carry the ID downstream and test the log contract

readings.takeaway: Accept a well-formed incoming request ID or generate one, log after c.Next with c.FullPath, status, latency and the ID, put redaction in ReplaceAttr so every record passes through it, and register the logger outside Recovery so failed requests are logged too.
readings.title: Request IDs and access logs in Gin: log the route template and the ID, never the credential
wrongAnswers: c.Request.URL.String(), so the query string is kept
c.Request.URL.Path, the exact path the client sent

cautions: Code that ignores ctx keeps running after the deadline.
Passing c as a context drops the deadline unless fallback is on.
designGuide.cost: A timer per request and the discipline of threading ctx through every call; dependencies that cannot be canceled still need their own timeouts.
strengths: One budget per request, inherited by every cooperating call.
A single goroutine writes the response, so nothing races.

readings.hint: Look for the engine flag that Context.Done checks before it delegates.
readings.introduction: A request stuck on a slow dependency holds a goroutine, a connection and often a database slot. A deadline bounds that wait, but only if every call below the handler receives the context that carries it. Deadlines are cooperative: Go cannot stop a goroutine from outside, so the safe design lets the handler notice expiry and write the response itself instead of racing it from another goroutine.
readings.nuance: Context.Done delegates to c.Request.Context() only when engine.ContextWithFallback is true. The default is false, so a dependency that waits on c never sees the deadline.
readings.objective: Give each request a deadline that downstream calls inherit, map its expiry to 504, and avoid the timeout patterns that race on the response.
readings.question: In Gin v1.12.0, with an engine from gin.New(), what does c.Done() return in a handler whose request context has a deadline?
readings.reviewAnswer: nil: no fallback to the request context

sections.body: http.Server's ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout bound connection I/O; they do not cancel your handler or the query it started. net/http cancels the request context when the client disconnects, when an HTTP/2 stream is reset, or when ServeHTTP returns. How long an answer is still worth computing is an application decision, so set the deadline in middleware where it is uniform and visible. Keep it below the timeout of the client or proxy in front of you, so your own 504 arrives before their generic error, and leave time for writing the response. Downstream calls must receive c.Request.Context(), not context.Background(), or the budget stops at the handler. A child call may tighten the deadline with its own WithTimeout, but it can never extend the parent's.
sections.title: Decide who owns the budget

sections.body: The middleware derives a context with a 20 ms budget, replaces c.Request with a copy that carries it, and cancels the context when the chain returns. The store models a dependency that respects its context; the hung variant never answers, so only the deadline can end the call. The last two requests inspect the context.Context methods of *gin.Context itself, with ContextWithFallback off and then on.
sections.title: Wrap the request context and pass it down
sections.walkthrough: c.Request.WithContext returns a shallow copy of the request, and assigning it to c.Request makes every later c.Request.Context() call see the deadline. defer cancel releases the timer as soon as the chain returns, including on success. getNote maps context.DeadlineExceeded to 504 and context.Canceled to 499, nginx's non-standard code for a client that closed the request, which only labels the log because nobody reads that response. The hung store returns once the 20 ms budget expires. The pre-canceled request shows that a derived context inherits cancellation: the WithTimeout child is already done, and Err reports Canceled, not DeadlineExceeded. In the inspect lines, the default engine reports no deadline and a nil Done channel even though c.Request.Context() has a deadline.

sections.body: *gin.Context implements context.Context, so store.Lookup(c, id) compiles. In Gin v1.12.0 its Deadline, Done and Err delegate to c.Request.Context() only when engine.ContextWithFallback is true, and gin.New leaves it false. With the default, Done returns a nil channel, which never becomes ready in a select, and Err always returns nil, so a dependency waiting on c ignores both your deadline and the client's disconnect; against the hung store it would never return. Value splits the same way: string keys are looked up in c.Keys first, and any key not found there reaches the request context only when fallback is on, so trace spans stored by other middleware silently vanish. Pass c.Request.Context() explicitly; it is clear in review and works with any engine. If you also set ContextWithFallback, do it once at startup. Note too that c.Copy keeps the same Request and therefore the same cancellation. That is fine for a short read, but detached work needs its own context; context.WithoutCancel keeps the values and drops the cancellation, as the context-workers lesson discusses.
sections.title: Why passing c as the context is a trap

sections.body: A popular timeout middleware runs c.Next in a goroutine, waits on a timer, and writes 504 itself if the timer fires first. Two goroutines now own one response: the handler may still be writing headers or a body while the middleware writes the 504, which is a data race on the ResponseWriter and can send a mixed or duplicated response. Gin makes it worse. As soon as the middleware returns, engine.ServeHTTP puts the *gin.Context back into a sync.Pool, and the next request can receive it while the abandoned handler goroutine is still using it. This is the retention bug from the context-workers lesson, hidden inside middleware. net/http's TimeoutHandler does this safely because it gives the handler a buffered, mutex-protected writer and decides the final response itself. The price is that it buffers the whole body, does not support Flusher, so streaming is impossible, and always answers 503 on timeout. A Gin access log running inside it also records the handler's status, not the 503 the client received. The cooperative design here keeps one writer: the handler notices the deadline and writes the answer.
sections.title: Never write the response from a second goroutine

sections.body: 504 Gateway Timeout says a dependency did not answer in time. 503 Service Unavailable, ideally with Retry-After, says the service chose not to do the work, for example because a queue was full or the budget was gone before the work started. Pick one convention and document it for clients. Check ctx.Err() before expensive steps so a request with almost no budget left fails fast, and never start a retry after the deadline has passed. Cancellation reaches only code that looks for it: a database driver can cancel a query only through QueryContext and friends, and a CPU-bound loop must check ctx itself. Test the fast path, a hung dependency, a request canceled before it starts, and a dependency that ignores its context. That last case shows the limit of cooperative cancellation, because the request returns late and the goroutine leaks. Run the suite under the race detector.
sections.title: Choose the status and test the edges

readings.takeaway: Derive a per-request deadline in middleware, pass c.Request.Context() to every downstream call, map DeadlineExceeded to 504 and Canceled to a log label, and let only the handler goroutine write the response. Do not use *gin.Context as a context unless ContextWithFallback is on.
readings.title: Request deadlines in Gin: one context budget, cooperative handlers, no writes from a second goroutine
wrongAnswers: The Done channel of c.Request.Context()
A channel that closes when the handler returns

cautions: WriteTimeout cuts long streams unless you set per-write deadlines.
Shutdown does not cancel streams; give them a stop signal.
designGuide.cost: One goroutine and one connection per subscriber for the whole session, plus a replay store if clients must resume without gaps.
strengths: Plain HTTP: works through proxies, with automatic reconnects.
An explicit select loop is deterministic under httptest.

readings.hint: Read the first lines of Context.Stream, then list the interfaces ResponseRecorder implements.
readings.introduction: Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and append small text events to it; the browser's EventSource parses them and reconnects on its own. The protocol is simple, and the engineering is all in the lifecycle. Every event must be flushed through buffers, idle streams need heartbeats, the handler must notice when the client leaves, and the server's write deadline must not cut the stream short.
readings.nuance: Stream calls c.Writer.CloseNotify(), which type-asserts the underlying writer to http.CloseNotifier. ResponseRecorder does not implement it, so the assertion panics, and tests need a loop on the request context instead.
readings.objective: Stream SSE from a Gin handler that flushes events, sends heartbeats, ends when the client leaves and survives http.Server's WriteTimeout.
readings.question: What happens in Gin v1.12.0 when a handler that calls c.Stream is exercised with httptest.NewRecorder()?
readings.reviewAnswer: It panics: the recorder lacks CloseNotify

sections.body: An event is a group of field lines ended by a blank line: event: names it, data: carries the payload, and optional id: and retry: lines support reconnection. A line that starts with a colon is a comment that EventSource ignores, which makes it a cheap heartbeat. In Gin v1.12.0, c.SSEvent(name, data) renders through gin-contrib/sse. It sets Content-Type to text/event-stream;charset=utf-8, sets Cache-Control: no-cache unless a value is already present, writes the event: and data: lines, turns newlines inside string data into extra data: lines, and JSON-encodes structs, maps and slices. It never writes an id: line. It also mostly swallows write failures: string payloads ignore them, and a failed JSON write only lands in c.Errors. The handler therefore cannot learn from SSEvent that the client has gone, and has to watch the request context instead.
sections.title: The wire format and what c.SSEvent writes

sections.body: c.Stream(step) loops: it checks the channel returned by c.Writer.CloseNotify(), calls step, flushes, and stops when step returns false. Two consequences follow from the v1.12.0 code. Gin's CloseNotify is an unchecked type assertion on the underlying writer, and httptest.ResponseRecorder does not implement http.CloseNotifier, so under a recorder c.Stream panics with a missing method CloseNotify error. Disconnects are also checked only between steps, so a step that blocks waiting for the next event leaves a departed client unnoticed until something is published. net/http deprecates CloseNotifier in favor of Request.Context for exactly this reason. On a real server c.Stream works if the step itself selects on the request context.
sections.title: What c.Stream does, read from the source
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs inside a handler on a real http.Server in your own environment, where the response writer implements CloseNotify. The select inside step makes a disconnect end the stream immediately instead of at the next event. The boolean result reports whether Stream saw CloseNotify fire. Under httptest.NewRecorder the same handler panics before step is ever called, which is why the tested version below uses its own loop.

sections.body: The handler below does the same work with one select over the request context, the event feed and a heartbeat channel. It commits headers with an early flush and uses http.ResponseController to replace the server-wide WriteTimeout with a deadline per write. The test feeds the handler from one goroutine over unbuffered channels, so exactly one select case is ready at any moment and the output is deterministic. Canceling the request context simulates the client disconnecting.
sections.title: An explicit loop that tests cleanly
sections.walkthrough: The Flush before the first event sends the status and headers, so EventSource fires its open event right away instead of waiting for data. The two-line note becomes two data: lines, the gin.H value is JSON-encoded with sorted keys, and : ping is a comment the browser discards. Result() reports the headers as they were when first written, so it shows the handler's text/event-stream rather than the variant SSEvent later writes into the header map. After disconnect(), ctx.Done is the only ready case, so the handler and ServeHTTP return. The last line shows that the recorder cannot set write deadlines: SetWriteDeadline returns an error matching http.ErrNotSupported, which the handler tolerates. The deadline itself needs a native integration test.

sections.body: http.Server.WriteTimeout sets one deadline on the connection after the request headers are read, and writes do not extend it. A stream that outlives it gets write errors, and clients reconnect in a loop at exactly that interval. Setting WriteTimeout to zero for the whole server removes the protection from every normal route. Instead, call SetWriteDeadline on a ResponseController before each write. The stream can then last for hours, while a client that stops reading can hold the goroutine for at most one write budget. This works through Gin's writer because ResponseController follows its Unwrap method. Heartbeats every 15 to 30 seconds keep load balancers with idle timeouts from closing quiet streams, and buffering proxies need buffering disabled for the route, for example nginx's X-Accel-Buffering: no response header. Shutdown waits for active connections to go idle and does not cancel request contexts, so an open stream blocks it until the shutdown budget expires. Use RegisterOnShutdown to close a stop channel that every stream loop selects on.
sections.title: WriteTimeout, proxies and shutdown

sections.body: EventSource reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID with the last id: it received. Resuming without gaps needs IDs from a durable sequence that the server can replay from. Because c.SSEvent has no id parameter, write the id: line yourself, or render a gin-contrib/sse Event with Id set through c.Render. Each stream costs one goroutine and one connection, so cap concurrent streams per user and in total; a reload loop or a forgotten tab adds up quickly. Over HTTP/1.1, browsers allow about six connections per origin across all tabs, while HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection. With in-process fan-out, a slow subscriber must not block the publisher: give each subscriber a small buffered channel and disconnect it when the buffer is full, then let it resume from Last-Event-ID. Test event formatting including newlines, heartbeats, a disconnect, a closed feed and a shutdown signal, and verify write deadlines against a real listener.
sections.title: Resume, fan-out and limits

readings.takeaway: Commit headers with a flush, write each event with c.SSEvent and flush it, send comment heartbeats, and select on c.Request.Context().Done() instead of relying on c.Stream's CloseNotify check. Replace the server-wide WriteTimeout with a per-write deadline from ResponseController.
readings.title: Server-Sent Events in Gin: flush every event, send heartbeats, stop on the request context
wrongAnswers: It streams normally and ResponseRecorder.Flushed is true
c.Stream returns true at once, reporting a disconnect

cautions: Dependency checks in liveness turn outages into restart storms.
Raw paths or client-chosen methods as labels grow without bound.
designGuide.cost: Two small endpoints, one middleware and a bounded map; a real metrics stack adds a client library and storage for every series you create.
strengths: Probes tell the platform exactly what to do: restart or reroute.
Route-template labels keep metric cardinality fixed.

readings.hint: Ask what the platform does when liveness fails on every replica at the same moment.
readings.introduction: Health endpoints and request counters are how the platform and the on-call engineer see a service from outside. Each answers a narrow question: should this process be restarted, should it receive traffic right now, and how is each route behaving. Mixing up the first two causes restart storms. Labeling counters with raw paths makes the metrics system the next thing to fall over.
readings.nuance: A failed liveness probe triggers a restart. Restarting every replica cannot repair the database and adds reconnect load, while a failed readiness probe only takes the replica out of traffic.
readings.objective: Separate liveness from readiness, check dependencies within a short budget, and count requests by route template and status class.
readings.question: Should a service's liveness probe fail when its database is unreachable?
readings.reviewAnswer: No: a restart cannot fix it and causes storms

sections.body: An orchestrator such as Kubernetes restarts a container whose liveness probe fails, and stops routing traffic to one whose readiness probe fails without restarting it. If liveness checks the database, a database outage makes every replica fail liveness at once. The platform restarts all of them, the restarts add a reconnect storm to a struggling database, and the outage lasts longer. So liveness checks only what a restart can fix: the process is serving HTTP and is not wedged. Readiness checks what traffic needs: required dependencies are reachable, startup work is finished, and the replica is not draining. During shutdown, readiness turns false first so the load balancer stops sending new requests before the server drains, as the server-lifecycle lesson describes. Kubernetes HTTP probes treat any status from 200 to 399 as success, so return a 5xx code to mean not ready.
sections.title: Liveness and readiness answer different questions

sections.body: readiness runs every check concurrently under one 25 ms context, so a hung dependency costs one budget rather than one per check and cannot starve the others. countRequests records the normalized method, route template and status class after c.Next. The traffic includes three user IDs, two scanner paths and a nonsense method, followed by probes before and after a simulated database outage and during a drain.
sections.title: A budgeted readiness check and route-keyed counters
sections.walkthrough: wg.Go, available since Go 1.25, starts each check, and each check writes only its own slot in errs, so no mutex is needed and the failed list keeps the configured order. The hung database blocks until the budget expires and is reported by name. The body leaves out the error text, because probe responses are often reachable from outside and internal hostnames do not belong there. Liveness answers 200 throughout, and draining short-circuits readiness before any check runs. countRequests labels by c.FullPath, so /users/1, /users/2 and /users/3 collapse into one series, the scanner paths become unmatched, and BREW becomes OTHER because the method string is client-controlled too. WriteText copies the map under the lock and sorts it, because map iteration order is random.

sections.body: Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series that the metrics backend must store, index and query. Label by raw path, and every user ID, order number and scanner probe mints a new series. A crawler or a hostile client can create millions of them in an hour, which shows up as memory growth in your process, where the counter map lives, and again in the backend, where dashboards slow to a crawl. Prometheus's naming guidance is explicit: do not use labels for unbounded values such as user IDs or email addresses. Keep labels to bounded sets: the route template, a normalized method and the status class, or a short list of exact codes you actually alert on. Put the specifics in logs and traces, keyed by request ID, where high cardinality is expected and affordable. Status classes are enough for error-rate alerts; add exact codes when a dashboard has to tell 404 apart from 429.
sections.title: Why raw paths explode metric cardinality

sections.body: A readiness probe runs every few seconds on every replica, so keep it cheap: a ping with a short timeout, not a real query against a large table. One shared budget, set below the probe's own timeout, guarantees the endpoint answers in time. A probe that times out is still a failure, but it tells you nothing about which dependency caused it. Consider caching the result for a second or two, or running the checks in a background goroutine and letting /readyz read the latest result, so a burst of probes cannot add load to a struggling dependency. Include only dependencies without which the replica cannot serve anything. If a recommendations service is optional, degrade that feature instead of going unready; otherwise one optional outage removes the whole fleet from rotation, which is the liveness cascade again in a different form. Serve probes on an internal port where you can, and keep their bodies minimal.
sections.title: Give readiness checks a budget and restraint

sections.body: Counters models what a metrics client does: a concurrency-safe map from a bounded label set to a number, exported in a text format. A real client adds latency histograms, which count observations per bucket, process metrics and the exact exposition format with label escaping. The standard library's expvar package is an option for simple counters, but importing it registers /debug/vars on http.DefaultServeMux and publishes the command line and memory statistics, so serve it only on an internal listener. Whichever you choose, keep the metrics endpoint off the public router. Tests should check that requests for different IDs share one series, that unmatched paths and unknown methods are bucketed, that readiness fails within its budget when a dependency hangs, that liveness stays 200 throughout, and that the counter survives parallel requests under the race detector.
sections.title: From the model counter to a real metrics stack

readings.takeaway: Keep liveness free of dependency checks. Let readiness check required dependencies concurrently within a short budget and report draining. Label request counters only with bounded values: route template, normalized method and status class.
readings.title: Health and metrics in Gin: simple liveness, budgeted readiness, counters keyed by route template
wrongAnswers: Yes, so the platform restarts into a healthy state
Yes, liveness and readiness should run the same checks

cautions: public on per-user data lets shared caches leak it.
Hashing still renders the full response; it saves bandwidth, not work.
designGuide.cost: A SHA-256 over each response body and a few header checks; version-based validators save more but need a reliable version source.
strengths: Unchanged responses cost a header round trip, not a body.
Byte-derived ETags are always correct, even for same-second edits.

readings.hint: Check which Cache-Control directives allow a shared cache to reuse a response to an authenticated request.
readings.introduction: A conditional GET lets a client that already holds a copy ask whether it is still current. When it is, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, which saves bandwidth and the client's parsing time. The mechanism has three parts: a validator on every response, a comparison on every request, and a Cache-Control policy that decides who may keep a copy. The policy is where private data leaks.
readings.nuance: RFC 9111 lets a shared cache reuse a response to a request with Authorization only when directives such as public allow it. Adding public removes that protection, so the CDN can replay one user's data to the next.
readings.objective: Serve ETag and Last-Modified validators, answer conditional requests with 304, and choose Cache-Control so private data never lands in a shared cache.
readings.question: A per-user /me response is sent with Cache-Control: public, max-age=60 behind a CDN. What can go wrong?
readings.reviewAnswer: Shared caches may serve it to other users

sections.body: An ETag is an opaque, quoted identifier for one representation of a resource. A strong ETag such as "a1fe" promises byte-for-byte identity, while a weak one such as W/"a1fe" promises only semantic equivalence. Last-Modified is a date with one-second resolution. Clients send them back as If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since. The order matters: when If-None-Match is present, the server evaluates it and ignores If-Modified-Since, and the date is consulted only when no ETag condition was sent. If-None-Match uses the weak comparison, so W/"x" matches "x". A 304 must carry the ETag, Cache-Control, Vary and Expires headers that a 200 would have carried, so a cache can refresh the metadata of its stored copy. This handling applies to GET and HEAD. For state-changing methods, a failed If-None-Match means 412 Precondition Failed, and If-Match is the tool for optimistic concurrency on updates.
sections.title: Validators and the order RFC 9110 prescribes

sections.body: serve renders the value to bytes once, derives a strong ETag from the SHA-256 of those bytes, and sets the validators and caching headers before it decides between a bodiless 304 and a 200 carrying the bytes. The requests cover a first fetch, revalidation by ETag in strong and weak form, revalidation by date, an edit made 400 ms after the previous one, and a private endpoint.
sections.title: Hash the bytes, compare, then send 200 or 304
sections.walkthrough: strongETag quotes the first 12 bytes of the SHA-256 digest in hex; 96 bits makes an accidental collision between versions of one resource irrelevant. Because the ETag names the exact bytes, any change to the JSON changes it. matches splits the header's list, strips W/ to perform the weak comparison and accepts *. notModified checks If-None-Match first and looks at If-Modified-Since only when it is absent, truncating the modification time to whole seconds as the header format does. The edited article shows why the order matters. The edit happened within the same second, so the date check wrongly answers 304. Worse, that 304 carries the new ETag, so a cache would pair the old body with the new validator and keep revalidating it successfully. The ETag check returns the new 82 bytes. c.Status(304) leaves the body empty, and Gin writes the header when the chain ends.

sections.body: Validators say whether a copy is current; Cache-Control says who may keep one and for how long. public, max-age=60 lets any cache, including CDNs and shared proxies, serve the response for 60 seconds without asking and then revalidate with the ETag, which suits data that is identical for every caller. private, no-cache lets only the user's own browser store the response and requires revalidation before each use, which suits per-user data where a 304 still saves the body. no-store forbids keeping a copy at all, which suits tokens, payment details and anything you would not want in a shared computer's disk cache. Note that no-cache does not mean do not cache; it means do not reuse without revalidating. Under RFC 9111, a shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with an Authorization header unless the response explicitly allows it with public, s-maxage or must-revalidate. Adding public to a per-user response therefore removes exactly the protection that kept the CDN from serving it to the next user. HTTP gives cookie-authenticated responses no such default, so mark them private explicitly, and list every request header that changes the response in Vary.
sections.title: Cache-Control for public and private data

sections.body: Hashing the rendered bytes is simple and always correct, but the server still loads and renders everything, so a 304 saves bandwidth and client parsing, not database time. When rendering is expensive, derive the validator from a version instead: a row version, or an update timestamp with sub-second precision, combined with whatever shapes the representation, such as API version, language or selected fields. That lets the handler answer 304 before loading the full object. A strong ETag names one representation, including its content coding, so if middleware gzips the body, the compressed bytes need a different strong ETag, or a weak one. Serialization must be deterministic for byte hashing to work. encoding/json sorts map keys, but a hand-written encoder that ranges over a map does not, and every response would then look new. ETags are visible to clients, so never build them from secrets. For files and blobs, http.ServeContent implements If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since and Range for you once you set the ETag header.
sections.title: Where the ETag should come from

sections.body: Assert that the first fetch returns an ETag and the intended Cache-Control. A matching If-None-Match should give 304 with an empty body and the same validators. A weak form, a list of several tags and * should all match, and a different tag should give 200. If-Modified-Since alone should work, If-None-Match should take precedence over it, and a same-second edit should be detected. Private routes must never say public, and routes whose output depends on Authorization must list it in Vary. HEAD should behave like GET without a body. The most valuable test runs in a staging environment behind the real CDN: request a private resource as user A, then as user B, and confirm that B never receives A's body. That single check catches the configuration mistakes that unit tests of the handler cannot see.
sections.title: Test the contract, not just the 200

readings.takeaway: Compute a strong ETag from the exact response bytes or a precise version, check If-None-Match before If-Modified-Since, answer 304 with the same validators and caching headers but no body, and mark per-user data private or no-store so shared caches never serve it to someone else.
readings.title: Conditional GETs in Gin: strong ETags from response bytes, 304 Not Modified and safe Cache-Control
wrongAnswers: Nothing: the Authorization header keeps it private
Only the ETag leaks; the body is never cached

cautions: Splitting into many tiny packages early adds ceremony without protection.
Package-level globals or os.Getenv calls inside internal packages defeat the layout.
designGuide.cost: A few more files and constructor calls than a single main.go; the payoff starts with the first test that needs a fake store.
strengths: Business rules can be tested and reused without HTTP or a database.
A new storage backend or transport is a new adapter plus a line in main.
The import graph documents the architecture and can be checked in CI.

readings.hint: Look for the one function that names concrete types such as MemoryStore.
readings.introduction: One main.go holding handlers, SQL and business rules works until the first test, the second developer or the second storage backend. This unit grows a single notes API over nine lessons, so this first lesson fixes where each piece lives. Later lessons then add CRUD, pagination, problem details, idempotency and versioning without moving code between packages.
readings.nuance: Only the composition root knows every concrete type. The adapters import the domain and the domain imports nothing from the project, so swapping a store changes main and nothing else.
readings.objective: Organize a Gin API into cmd/api, httpapi, notes and store packages whose imports point toward the domain, with all concrete wiring in main.
readings.question: In the notes API layout, which package is allowed to import the store, the HTTP adapter and the domain together?
readings.reviewAnswer: Only cmd/api, the composition root

sections.body: The layout follows the server-project shape from the Go documentation: commands under cmd, everything else under internal. Inside internal the split is by responsibility, not by technical layer. notes is the domain: the Note type, the errors callers can test for, the Service with the business rules and the Store interface the service needs. store holds adapters that satisfy that interface. httpapi turns HTTP requests into service calls and service results into responses. cmd/api/main.go is the composition root that builds and connects them. The rule that keeps this from decaying is the direction of imports: both adapters import notes, notes imports neither, and only main imports everything.
sections.code:
notes-api/
  go.mod                    module example.com/notes-api
  cmd/
    api/
      main.go               composition root: config, wiring, http.Server
  internal/
    notes/                  domain: Note, error values, Service, Store interface
      note.go
      errors.go
      service.go
    store/                  adapters that implement notes.Store
      memory.go
      postgres.go
    httpapi/                Gin adapter: handlers, routes, error mapping
      handler.go
      routes.go
      problems.go
      handler_test.go
    config/                 environment parsing and validation

imports:
  cmd/api       -> config, httpapi, notes, store, gin
  httpapi       -> notes, gin
  store         -> notes, a database driver
  notes         -> standard library only
sections.title: Four packages and one direction of imports
sections.walkthrough: The tree is the real module the rest of the unit builds. internal/ is enforced by the go command: only code rooted at notes-api/ may import these packages, so nothing outside the module can couple to them. The imports block is the dependency graph to defend in review. If store ever needs something from httpapi, or notes needs Gin, the arrow points the wrong way and the design, not the compiler, is the thing to fix.

sections.body: The runnable model keeps the same boundaries but folds the four packages into one file, with a comment where each package would begin. Read the types as if they were in separate directories: Note, the errors, Store and Service belong to notes; MemoryStore belongs to store; NoteService, Handler, NewRouter and writeError belong to httpapi; main is cmd/api. The program wires the pieces once and sends four requests through the engine with ServeHTTP.
sections.title: The whole service in one runnable file
sections.walkthrough: The domain trims the title and rejects an empty or overlong one with ErrInvalid; that rule lives in Service, so a CLI or a queue consumer would get it too. MemoryStore satisfies Store without naming it, and it returns ErrNotFound from the domain package rather than inventing its own error. The Handler depends on NoteService, an interface listing the two calls it makes, so httpapi never sees MemoryStore. main is the only function that names every concrete type: it builds the ID source, the store, the service and the router, in that order. The output shows a created note, a read, a 422 for a blank title and a 404, all mapped in writeError, which the problem-details lesson later moves into one middleware.

sections.body: The composition root reads configuration, constructs concrete adapters, connects them through constructors and owns the process lifecycle: starting the server, handling signals and calling os.Exit. It should read like a wiring diagram, a few dozen lines with no business decisions. Everything else moves out. Packages under internal should not call os.Getenv, parse flags, open connections in init, keep package-level singletons or call log.Fatal. Each of those hides an input or an exit path from the caller and makes the package impossible to test in isolation. When a package needs a setting, it takes it as a constructor argument or a field; when it fails, it returns an error and lets main decide whether that ends the process. The config-and-startup lesson at the end of this unit fills in main completely.
sections.title: What belongs in main, and what never does

sections.body: Package-by-layer trees such as models, controllers and services look organized, but every package imports models, everything is exported to cross the boundaries, and a change to one feature touches all of them. A utils or common package becomes the place where unrelated code goes to import each other. A domain function that accepts *gin.Context or returns gin.H has quietly made Gin part of the business rules, so a background job now needs a fake HTTP request. An httpapi handler that imports store directly to save a layer bypasses the service and its rules. A top-level pkg directory in a service that no other module imports adds a path segment and no protection; internal already says what it means. Start with few packages named for what they provide, and split one only when it has a second reason to change.
sections.title: Layouts that look tidy and still couple everything

sections.body: Go refuses to compile an import cycle, so the most damaging mistakes surface early, but a one-way dependency in the wrong direction compiles fine. Make the intended graph visible and cheap to check. go list prints each package with its imports, and a short pipeline can fail a CI job when the domain starts depending on Gin or on an adapter. Review a new import in notes with the same care as a new dependency in go.mod.
sections.code:
# Each package in the module and what it imports.
go list -f '{{.ImportPath}} -> {{join .Imports " "}}' ./...

# The domain must not depend on Gin, a store or the HTTP adapter.
go list -deps ./internal/notes \
  | grep -E 'gin-gonic|notes-api/internal/(store|httpapi)' \
  && echo "layering violation" || echo "notes is clean"
sections.title: Check the direction of imports in review
sections.walkthrough: Run these commands in your own checkout of the module. The first prints one line per package, for example "example.com/notes-api/internal/store -> context example.com/notes-api/internal/notes sync", which is exactly the arrow the layout promises. The second lists every transitive dependency of internal/notes and searches it for Gin or the two adapter packages; any match prints "layering violation", and a CI step can turn that into a failing exit code.

readings.takeaway: Keep internal/notes free of Gin and storage imports, let the HTTP and storage adapters import the domain, and confine concrete wiring, configuration and os.Exit to cmd/api/main.go.
readings.title: Lay out a Gin service so every import points toward the domain
wrongAnswers: internal/notes, so the service can build its own store
internal/httpapi, so handlers can open the database

cautions: A typed nil pointer inside an interface passes a nil check.
Hand-written fakes need a mutex if tests share them across goroutines.
designGuide.cost: Constructor parameters and a few small interfaces; main grows by a handful of lines per dependency.
strengths: Every collaborator is visible in one struct and one constructor call.
Tests run the real router with a fake store, clock and IDs.
Missing wiring fails at startup or at compile time, not on a request.

readings.hint: Ask which package needs to replace the dependency in its tests.
readings.introduction: A handler that reaches for a package-level database variable works on the first day and fights you afterwards: tests share state, parallel tests race, and no signature tells a reviewer what the handler can touch. Passing dependencies through a constructor makes them visible, replaceable and checked by the compiler. This lesson does that for the notes API, including the clock and the ID source.
readings.nuance: The consumer knows which methods it calls. Declaring the interface there keeps it small, leaves the provider concrete and avoids an import from the domain back to the adapter.
readings.objective: Write handlers as methods on a struct built by a constructor, depend on small consumer-defined interfaces and swap in a fake store for tests.
readings.question: In the notes API, which package should declare the NoteService interface that the HTTP handlers depend on?
readings.reviewAnswer: In the package that consumes them

sections.body: Both shapes below compile and serve requests. The first keeps the store in a package variable, so every test in the package shares one instance, a test that forgets to reset it leaks data into the next, and t.Parallel turns that into a race. The second hides the dependency in the Gin context: some middleware must call c.Set first, the type assertion moves a compile-time fact to run time, and a forgotten Use call becomes a panic on the first request rather than a build error. time.Now and an unseeded random ID generator are hidden globals of the same kind; they are why a response body cannot be compared byte for byte in a test.
sections.title: What globals and context lookups cost
sections.walkthrough: This fragment shows what to avoid and is not meant to compile on its own. getNote has no parameters that mention storage, so a reader must search the package to learn where db is assigned. getNoteFromContext depends on a string key and a concrete type assertion; renaming the key or changing the type is not caught until a request hits the route. Request-scoped values such as the authenticated user do belong in the context; long-lived dependencies do not.

sections.body: The notes service now takes three dependencies in its constructor: a Store, a clock and an ID source. The HTTP Handler takes a NoteService and a *slog.Logger. Register attaches method values such as h.getNote to any gin.IRouter, so the same handler works on an engine or a route group. The test half of the file builds the same graph with a fake store, a fixed clock and sequential IDs, then runs a healthy and a failing scenario through the real router.
sections.title: Handlers as methods, dependencies as fields
sections.walkthrough: NewService refuses a nil dependency, so the first output line is a wiring error at startup instead of a nil-pointer panic during a request. With the healthy fake, GET returns the seeded note and POST creates n1 with the fixed timestamp 2026-01-02T03:04:05Z, which is why the body is stable enough to compare. The fake records every call, so the test can assert that the handler asked for n7 and inserted n1 without inspecting private state. The broken fake returns a dial error: the handler logs the cause through its injected logger (the time attribute is dropped to keep output stable) and the client receives only a generic 500 body.

sections.body: httpapi declares NoteService with exactly the two methods its handlers call, and notes declares Store with exactly what the service calls. The concrete types never mention these interfaces; Go satisfies them implicitly, which is what lets the consumer own the definition. That keeps interfaces small, so a fake is a dozen lines, and it keeps the import arrow pointing from adapter to domain. A provider-side interface with twenty methods that mirrors the store invites fakes that panic on the eighteen methods nobody meant to call. Constructors accept interfaces and return concrete types: NewService returns *Service, and each caller decides which slice of it to depend on. A one-line assertion keeps the provider and the consumer from drifting apart silently.
sections.title: Declare the interface where it is consumed
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in the module from the layout lesson and compiles there, not on its own. The blank-identifier assignment converts a typed nil *notes.Service to httpapi.NoteService at compile time; if someone renames Get or changes its signature, the build fails at this line with a message naming the missing method, instead of failing later where the router is wired. Exporting the interface is what makes this assertion possible from main.

sections.body: A constructor is the right place to reject an incomplete graph, because it runs once at startup where a clear error is cheap. One Go subtlety limits that check: a nil *MemoryStore stored in a Store interface is not equal to nil, so the guard only catches dependencies that were never assigned. For tests, prefer a small hand-written fake over a mocking framework: a map for state, an err field to inject failure and a calls slice to observe what happened. Assert outcomes such as the status, the body and the effect on the fake, not the exact order of every internal call, or the test breaks on every refactor. Build a new fake and a new router per test case; this fake has no mutex, which is fine only because nothing shares it. The API-tests lesson turns this into a full table.
sections.title: Constructors validate wiring; fakes control the world

sections.body: When a pull request adds a handler, three questions catch most dependency problems. Can the handler be constructed in a test without a network, a file or an environment variable? Does its struct list every collaborator it uses, including time and randomness? Is each interface field declared in the consuming package with only the methods it calls? If any answer is no, the missing piece is usually a constructor argument. The cost is a few more lines in main; the benefit is that every test from here on builds the real router with controlled edges.
sections.title: Review questions for a new handler

readings.takeaway: Build handlers from a struct whose fields are small interfaces declared by the consumer, inject the clock and ID source too, and let tests pass a fake store through the same constructor production uses.
readings.title: Give Gin handlers their dependencies through a struct, not globals or context keys
wrongAnswers: internal/notes, next to the concrete Service type
A shared interfaces package that every package imports

cautions: Pointer DTOs cannot distinguish an omitted field from an explicit null.
A store-level lock does not prevent lost updates between two clients.
designGuide.cost: Two DTOs per resource and an Update callback in the store; worth it as soon as a client sends partial updates.
strengths: Clients can rely on Location, 204 and 409 meaning the same thing everywhere.
Uniqueness is enforced where the data lives, so no check-then-write race.
PATCH can set false and empty values without ambiguity.

readings.hint: Compare what a plain bool holds when the field is missing and when it is false.
readings.introduction: CRUD looks like boilerplate until a client depends on the details: whether create tells it where the new note lives, whether PUT without a body field clears it, whether PATCH with false can unpin a note, and whether a duplicate title is a 400 or a 409. This lesson pins down each answer for the notes resource, on top of a mutex-protected in-memory store behind the Store interface.
readings.nuance: With a plain bool an omitted field and an explicit false both decode to false, so the handler cannot tell "leave it" from "unpin it". A nil pointer marks absence.
readings.objective: Implement create, read, replace, patch and delete for notes with correct status codes, a Location header and presence-aware PATCH fields.
readings.question: A PATCH request sends {"pinned":false}. Why does patchNote use *bool instead of bool for Pinned?
readings.reviewAnswer: nil means absent, so false and "" stay settable
readings.reviewPrompt: Why pointer fields in a PATCH DTO?

sections.body: A resource API is a promise about methods, paths, statuses and headers, and clients code against every part of it. Writing the table first exposes decisions that are easy to fudge in code: who assigns IDs, what a partial update means and which errors exist. Here the server assigns IDs, so POST creates and PUT only replaces an existing note. Titles are unique, which gives the store a real invariant to protect and the API a real reason to answer 409.
sections.code:
POST   /notes        create      201 Created + Location: /notes/{id} + body
                                 400 unreadable body, 409 title already used
GET    /notes/{id}   read        200 + body, 404 unknown id
PUT    /notes/{id}   replace     200 + body, 400 incomplete body, 404, 409
PATCH  /notes/{id}   merge       200 + body, 400 invalid field, 404, 409
DELETE /notes/{id}   remove      204 No Content (empty body), 404 unknown id
sections.title: Write the contract before the handlers
sections.walkthrough: Read each row as a test case. 201 always comes with a Location header pointing at the new resource, so clients never guess URLs. 204 means success with no body: the net/http server rejects a body write for it with http.ErrBodyNotAllowed, and Gin renderers skip the body for that status. 404 and 409 come from domain errors, not from handler logic. 400 is for input the adapter cannot accept; the binding-limits lesson already covers size limits and strict decoding, so this lesson only uses binding tags.

sections.body: The store keeps two maps that must always agree: notes by ID and a unique index from title to ID. Every method takes the mutex, and Update runs a caller-supplied function on a copy while holding the write lock, so read, modify and write happen as one step. Handlers translate HTTP into store calls and use a small writeError helper for now. The program replays a short session against the API and prints each status, Location header and body.
sections.title: Five routes over one locked store
sections.walkthrough: The first POST returns 201 with Location: /notes/n1.
