The key must therefore capture every input the handler reads, a request that carries identity must bypass the cache, and only a response that declares itself public may be stored. The conditional-requests lesson set Cache-Control and ETags for browsers and CDNs, which saves bandwidth. A server-side cache saves the handler's own work, the query and the render, and it lives inside your process, where you control the key, the lifetime and invalidation. The stampede and cache-aside lessons explain why concurrent misses are dangerous; this lesson builds the Gin middleware that handles them.
sections.title: The cache must never change the answer

sections.body: c.FullPath() returns the route template, such as /articles/:id, so the set of keys and the unit of invalidation follow routes rather than raw paths, and an unmatched request has an empty template and is never cached. Add the values from c.Params, then the query parsed with url.ParseQuery and re-encoded with Values.Encode, which sorts parameter names, so ?sort=new&page=1 and ?page=1&sort=new share an entry. Encode keeps the order of repeated values, because that order can be meaningful. Each route lists the parameters its handler reads. A request with any other parameter bypasses the cache instead of having the parameter dropped: dropping utm_source would be harmless, but dropping a parameter the handler does read would serve the wrong page. If you know some tracking parameters are ignored, strip them through a named list. Requests with Authorization or Cookie bypass, and a stored response must not carry Set-Cookie or Vary, because the key does not include the request headers it would vary on.
sections.title: Key by what the handler reads

sections.body: The program wraps one list route in the cache. A fake clock decides expiry. The handler counts its calls, reads the data version before doing slow work, and can be held at a gate so that misses overlap deterministically. The sequence covers a hit through a reordered query, three bypasses, a 304 served from the entry, a write, expiry, a write that lands during a fill, and two bursts of five concurrent misses, with and without coalescing.
sections.title: The middleware, a fake clock and a gated handler
sections.walkthrough: The first request misses and stores the response; ten seconds later the reordered query hits and Age reports 10. The bearer, cookie and utm requests bypass and each runs the handler. If-None-Match is answered 304 from the stored entry without a handler call. The POST bumps the version and invalidates /articles, so the next GET misses, and after the clock passes the 60 second TTL it misses again. In the write-during-a-fill step, the fill reads version 2 and waits; the POST invalidates the route meanwhile, so put discards the result and the next GET sees version 3 instead of a stale page for a minute. In the singleflight burst the gated leader is the only handler run: the other requests wait for it or hit the entry it stored. capture keeps its own header map, so headers that outer middleware set, such as a request ID, are never stored and replayed.

sections.body: group.Do runs the fill function on the calling goroutine, so the leader runs its own c.Next and no other goroutine ever touches its *gin.Context, as the context-fallback lesson requires. Followers block until the leader finishes and replay the same immutable entry onto their own writers, then Abort so their chains do not run. The fill re-checks the cache first, because a request that missed just before the previous flight ended would otherwise start a second fill. The flight key includes the route's generation, so a request that arrives after an invalidation never joins a flight that started before it. The limits are real. Do has no context, so a follower keeps waiting after its own client has gone; DoChan could select on cancellation, but it runs the function on a new goroutine, where calling c.Next would break the one-owner rule. If the leader's client disconnects and the handler fails, every follower receives that failed response, which at least is not stored. singleflight re-panics in the leader and in every follower; record restores the real writer in a defer so an outer Recovery can still answer 500, and registering Recovery inside the cache turns a panic into an ordinary 500 that is never stored. Coalescing is per process, so ten replicas still make ten fills.
sections.title: Coalescing misses inside Gin with singleflight

sections.body: A write handler commits and then invalidates the route templates whose responses it changed. Invalidating before the commit opens a window in which a read refills the entry with the old data. Even after the commit, a fill that read the old data before the write can finish afterwards and store it, which is the race the cache-aside lesson warns about. The per-route generation closes it: the fill captures the generation before running the handler, and put stores only if it is unchanged. Per-route invalidation is coarse but easy to verify; tagging entries by resource ID is finer and costs bookkeeping in every handler. This cache lives in one process, so other replicas keep their entries until the TTL ends unless you broadcast invalidations or move to a shared cache, which makes the TTL your honest bound on staleness. The model also lacks two things a real service adds: a cap on entry count and body size with eviction, and metrics for hit ratio and bypass reasons.
sections.title: Invalidate after the commit, and guard fills in flight

sections.body: The handler from the conditional-requests lesson derives its ETag from the response bytes, so a stored body and its validator always travel together. Before filling, the cache removes If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since from its copy of the request, so a leader that sent a validator cannot produce a bodiless 304 that would be stored or replayed to followers. On replay the cache compares If-None-Match with the stored ETag and answers 304 itself, carrying ETag and Cache-Control, without running the handler. The Age header tells downstream caches how old the copy already is, so public, max-age=60 still means sixty seconds in total rather than sixty more on top of the time it spent in your cache. Responses marked private or no-store are never stored. Test the X-Cache sequence for each rule above, use the fake clock instead of sleeping, hold the handler at a gate to make concurrent misses reproducible, race a write against a fill, and run the suite under go test -race.
sections.title: Stay consistent with ETags, Age and Cache-Control

readings.takeaway: Cache only public GETs whose every input is in the key: route template, path params and allow-listed query. Bypass identity, coalesce misses with singleflight on the request goroutine, and guard invalidation with a generation so in-flight fills cannot store stale data.
readings.title: Cache public GETs in Gin: key by route template, bypass identity, coalesce misses, invalidate on write
wrongAnswers: Cache it: the route template already identifies the content
Strip the header, then fill the cache as usual

cautions: One transaction per upload holds a pooled connection at the client's pace.
Partial mode needs idempotent rows so a resend does not duplicate.
designGuide.cost: A line reader, a per-row report and a transaction that stays open for the upload; large files usually graduate to an asynchronous job.
strengths: Memory is bounded by one line, not by the file.
Clients get a line number and reason for every rejected row.

readings.hint: Count how many times binding.JSON calls Decode before it validates.
readings.introduction: A bulk import receives the largest bodies your service will ever see, from clients that may have produced part of the file wrong. Reading it whole turns file size into memory, and one bad row into an unexplained 400. Newline-delimited JSON lets the handler work one record at a time: bound the request, bound each line, judge each row on its own, and tell the client exactly which lines were written.
readings.nuance: Gin's decodeJSON makes one Decode call and never checks for more input, so the remaining lines are never read. A per-line reader with a trailing-data check is what sees every record.
readings.objective: Build an NDJSON import endpoint that bounds the body and each line, validates rows one at a time and returns a per-line report whose status matches what was written.
readings.question: In Gin v1.12.0, what does c.ShouldBindJSON(&p) do when the request body is NDJSON holding many valid records?
readings.reviewAnswer: Binds the first line, returns nil, ignores the rest

sections.body: In Gin v1.12.0, c.ShouldBindJSON hands the body to binding.JSON, which makes a single Decode call and then validates. On an NDJSON body it binds the first record, returns nil and never reads the other lines; the last line of the program below shows exactly that. Binding a []Product from a JSON array works, but it holds the whole file as Go values before validation starts, and one type error fails the entire decode without a line number. io.ReadAll followed by a split has the same memory profile. One json.Decoder over the whole stream is closer, but it accepts records that span lines or share one, reports byte offsets instead of line numbers, buffers each value whole however large it is, and after a syntax error it keeps returning that error, so one broken line ends the import. NDJSON offers a framing to exploit: one JSON value per line, so each line can be read, decoded and judged on its own.
sections.title: Why ShouldBindJSON and io.ReadAll fail on a file

sections.body: The handler wraps the body in http.MaxBytesReader, reads it through a bufio.Reader whose buffer is exactly the line limit, and stops after maxRows rows. ReadSlice returns bufio.ErrBufferFull when a line does not fit; the loop then discards the rest of that line chunk by chunk, so an oversized record costs one buffer of memory and becomes a rejected row instead of a failed request. Each valid row goes into a transaction, and the mode decides whether it commits. main sends the same file in both modes, then a body over the cap, then the file to ShouldBindJSON.
sections.title: Three bounds: the body, each line and the row count
sections.walkthrough: Line 2 fails the gt=0 rule from its binding tag, line 3 carries a field the struct does not declare, and line 4 is a record cut short, which the decoder reports as io.ErrUnexpectedEOF rather than a syntax error. Line 5 is over 120 bytes and is never decoded at all. Line 6 is valid JSON but repeats the SKU from line 1, a rule only the handler can check. Line 7 is blank: skipped, but still counted, so the report uses the numbers an editor shows. With mode=all one rejected row rolls the transaction back and the answer is 422; with mode=partial the two valid rows commit with 200. The 25-line body trips MaxBytesReader partway through, the handler rolls back the rows it had already staged, and the catalog stays at two items.

sections.body: decodeRow gives every line its own json.Decoder. DisallowUnknownFields is set on that decoder alone, so the strictness applies to this endpoint without flipping the process-wide binding.EnableDecoderDisallowUnknownFields; the binding-limits lesson discusses when strict input is the right contract. A second Decode must return io.EOF, which rejects two values on one line yet tolerates the trailing carriage return of CRLF files, because JSON treats it as whitespace. Validation reuses the binding tags a ShouldBindJSON handler would use: binding.Validator is the StructValidator Gin itself calls, and ValidateStruct runs it on one row. Registering a tag-name function, as in the custom-validators lesson, makes errors say price_cents rather than PriceCents. encoding/json has no typed error for an unknown field, so the program trims the json: prefix from the message; keep that mapping in one function so a reworded message in a future release is a one-line fix.
sections.title: Decode one line strictly and reuse Gin's validator

sections.body: Decide what each status code promises and keep it true in both modes. 422 Unprocessable Content means nothing was written: in mode=all because at least one row was rejected, in mode=partial because no row was valid. 200 means every row the report marks valid was written. 413 means the request itself was too large, by bytes or by rows, and nothing was written in either mode, because a request-level failure must never leave half a file behind. 415 answers a body that is not application/x-ndjson, and 400 a bad mode or an empty file. Avoid 207 Multi-Status: it comes from WebDAV, whose body is an XML multistatus document, and generic clients attach no meaning to it in a JSON API. Default to all-or-nothing, because a client can retry it blindly. Partial mode suits large hand-edited files, but the client must read the report, and resending a corrected file has to be safe: make rows idempotent, for example an upsert keyed by SKU, and accept an Idempotency-Key for retries of the same request, as the idempotency-keys lesson describes.
sections.title: All-or-nothing or partial: give each status one meaning

sections.body: Tx stands in for a database transaction: the handler streams rows into it and never holds the file itself, and rolling back on every request-level error is what keeps a 413 honest. With PostgreSQL that is an INSERT per row or per batch inside one transaction, or COPY into a staging table followed by a single INSERT ... SELECT. The systems.transaction-boundary lesson explains why a use case rather than the handler should own that transaction; the program opens it in the handler only to stay short. A transaction that lasts as long as an upload runs at the client's pace: a slow client keeps a pooled connection and its locks busy, and http.Server.ReadTimeout, which covers reading the whole body, may cut the request off. http.ResponseController.SetReadDeadline can extend it for this route only. Past a few megabytes, store the file and process it as a job behind 202, which the async-jobs lesson builds. One detail of MaxBytesReader under Gin: net/http marks the connection for closing when the limit is hit only if it receives its own response writer, through an unexported method that c.Writer cannot forward. With c.Writer the server applies its general rule when the 413 is written instead: it drains up to 256 KiB of unread body or closes the connection.
sections.title: Let the database hold the pending rows

sections.body: Assert line numbers and reasons, not just counts. Cover a blank line, CRLF endings, a last line without a newline, a line exactly at the limit and one byte over, a record split across two lines, two records on one line, a UTF-8 byte order mark at the start, which makes line 1 invalid JSON unless you strip it deliberately, a body over the cap in each mode and a row count over maxRows. After every rejected request, assert that the store is unchanged. Wrap test bodies in testing/iotest.OneByteReader to prove the line reader copes with short reads, since a network delivers bytes in arbitrary chunks. From a shell, send files with --data-binary.
sections.code:
curl -i -X POST 'http://localhost:8080/products/import?mode=partial' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' \
  --data-binary @products.ndjson
sections.title: Test the framing, not only a happy file
sections.walkthrough: Run this against the service in your own development environment. --data-binary sends the file byte for byte; -d @products.ndjson would strip carriage returns and newlines, so the server would see one long line, reject it as over the line limit and, with no valid row, answer 422. -i prints the status line before the JSON report, so you can check that the status follows the rules above.

readings.takeaway: Cap the body with http.MaxBytesReader, read NDJSON one bounded line at a time, decode each line strictly and validate it with Gin's validator, and let the status say what was written: 422 nothing, 200 every valid row, 413 nothing because the request was too large.
readings.title: NDJSON imports in Gin: cap the body, decode one bounded line at a time, report each row by its line number
wrongAnswers: Returns an error because data follows the first value
Binds the last record, since each Decode overwrites p

cautions: Errors after the first byte cannot change the status code.
Pages read at different moments are not one snapshot.
designGuide.cost: A keyset query per page, a deliberate middleware order and a client contract for spotting truncation; strict consistency needs a long read-only transaction or a pre-built file.
strengths: Memory and query cost stay at one page for any export size.
Bytes flow from the start, so idle timeouts do not fire.

readings.hint: Read how CustomRecoveryWithWriter classifies a recovered error before it decides whether to call the handle function.
readings.introduction: An export of a million rows should cost the server one page of rows at a time, not a million rows of memory and a long silence before the first byte. Writing CSV straight into c.Writer and flushing after every page achieves that. It also changes the error model: once the first page is on the wire the status line has gone, so a database failure on page forty can no longer become a 500, and the handler needs another way to tell the client the file is incomplete.
readings.nuance: Recovery treats ErrAbortHandler like a broken pipe: it records the error, aborts the chain and returns normally, so net/http completes the chunked body. Re-panic from a middleware registered before Recovery.
readings.objective: Stream a large CSV from a Gin handler page by page with a safe download filename and formula-safe cells, and make a failure after the first byte visible to the client.
readings.question: In Gin v1.12.0, a streaming handler panics with http.ErrAbortHandler after its first page, under gin.Recovery(). What does the client receive?
readings.reviewAnswer: Recovery swallows it and the body ends cleanly

sections.body: The obvious export loads every row, renders the CSV into a buffer and calls c.Data. Memory grows with the export, the first byte waits for the last row, and proxies and browsers with idle timeouts can give up on a large account before anything arrives, while one query materializes the whole result. Streaming fixes all three: read one keyset page, write it, flush it, repeat. The pagination lesson explains why pages of rows after the last key stay fast and stable where OFFSET pages slow down and drift. Two buffers sit between csv.Writer.Write and the network. csv.NewWriter wraps its destination in a 4 KiB bufio.Writer, which csv.Writer.Flush empties into c.Writer, and net/http keeps a 2 KiB buffer of its own, which c.Writer.Flush pushes onto the connection. Calling both after each page keeps delivery steady; skipping the second leaves bytes waiting until net/http's buffer happens to fill.
sections.title: Build the file in memory and you pay three times

sections.body: The handler fetches the first page before it writes anything, sets the headers, then loops: write a page, flush both buffers, stop on a short page, a canceled context or a store error. main first prints the Content-Disposition values for three list names, then runs a full export, a client that disconnects during page one, a store that is down before the first byte and a store that fails on page two, once with Gin's Recovery alone and once with abortPassthrough in front of it.
sections.title: An export handler and the ways it can end
sections.walkthrough: Seven contacts at three per page take three queries; the third page is short, which ends the loop without a fourth. Every user-supplied cell that starts with =, +, -, @, tab, carriage return or line feed gains a leading apostrophe, and encoding/csv quotes the fields that contain commas or quotes and doubles the inner quotes. When the request context is canceled during page one, the handler still writes that page, then its next Page call returns the context error and the loop ends without querying again. A store that fails before the first byte still gets an honest 503. On page two the status is already 200, so the only signal left is the connection itself. With Recovery alone the response ends normally after four lines, which a client cannot tell from a complete export; with abortPassthrough the ErrAbortHandler panic reaches serve, which plays the part of net/http.

sections.body: Content-Disposition carries a filename the browser proposes to the user, so build it like any other output. exportName keeps letters, digits, spaces, hyphens and underscores, falls back to a fixed name when nothing usable is left or the result is too long, and appends the extension itself, so path separators and CR LF never reach the header. mime.FormatMediaType then picks the encoding: a bare token, a quoted string with escaped quotes for ASCII with spaces, or the RFC 2231 form filename*=utf-8'' with percent-encoding for anything else. RFC 6266 defines that filename* parameter for HTTP and current browsers read it. FormatMediaType returns an empty string for an invalid type or parameter name, so keep the fallback. Gin's c.FileAttachment is no substitute: it serves a file from disk, and for non-ASCII names v1.12.0 encodes with url.QueryEscape, which writes spaces as + that RFC 8187 decoding keeps literally, so the browser saves Zoë+list.csv. CSV injection is the second risk. Spreadsheet apps can evaluate a cell that starts with =, +, - or @ as a formula, and OWASP's list adds control characters such as tab and carriage return, so an exported note can build links that leak neighboring cells. OWASP recommends prefixing such cells with a single quote, as safeCell does, while the encoder handles quotes and separators inside the field. That changes the data, so apply it only to free-text columns from users, never to values you format yourself: a negative balance would become text. Offer JSON for machine consumers that need raw values.
sections.title: Filenames and cells are user input too

sections.body: The first flush sends the 200 and the headers. From then on Gin's responseWriter ignores WriteHeader, printing a warning only in debug mode, so a c.JSON(500, ...) in the error path would append a JSON object to the CSV and still report success. Two rules follow. First, do everything that can fail cheaply before the first byte: authorize, validate parameters and run the first query, which is why the store-down case can still answer 503. Second, make a late failure visible as truncation. A panic with http.ErrAbortHandler makes net/http close the connection without the final zero-length chunk on HTTP/1.1, or reset the stream on HTTP/2, so curl, browsers and HTTP libraries report an error instead of saving a short file; net/http also skips the stack trace for that value. The surprise is gin.Recovery: v1.12.0 classifies ErrAbortHandler with broken pipes, records it with c.Error, aborts the chain and returns normally, so net/http finishes the response cleanly. abortPassthrough, registered before Recovery, finds the recorded error after c.Next returns and panics again outside Recovery's reach. Log the failure with the request ID and the last key written. Programmatic clients can also check an HTTP trailer or a final row count, but browsers ignore trailers, so the abort is the signal that works everywhere.
sections.title: After the first byte, the status line is history

sections.body: net/http cancels the request context when the client disconnects or an HTTP/2 stream is reset. Pass that context to every query so the one in flight is canceled, and check it before the next page, or the handler keeps reading the database for nobody; a write error from csv.Writer.Error after Flush is the same signal from the other side. A long export also outlives http.Server.WriteTimeout, so renew the write deadline per page with ResponseController, as the SSE lesson does for event streams. Each page is its own statement, so the file is not a point-in-time snapshot: a row edited between pages shows whichever value its page saw. When the export must be consistent, read every page inside one read-only REPEATABLE READ transaction, which in PostgreSQL gives all its statements the same snapshot, and accept that a transaction open for the whole download delays vacuum. For very large or audited exports, generate the file as a job, which the async-jobs lesson builds, and serve the finished file with a Content-Length.
sections.title: Cancellation, write deadlines and one consistent snapshot
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs against a real PostgreSQL database in your own environment. BeginTx with LevelRepeatableRead and ReadOnly pins one snapshot for every page, and the deferred Rollback releases it, which is all a read-only transaction needs. nextPage renews the write deadline before each page, tolerating http.ErrNotSupported from writers that cannot set one, then selects rows strictly after the last ID. With an index on (account_id, id), every page is a short range scan however deep into the export it is.

sections.body: Parse the body back with csv.NewReader and compare records rather than raw text, so a quoting change does not break tests while a content change does. Include hostile cells for every formula prefix, embedded commas, quotes and newlines, a non-ASCII list name, and page boundaries: zero rows, exactly one page, one row more than a page. Cancel mid-stream and assert that the store stopped being called, and fail both before and after the first byte. Build the test engine with the same middleware order as production, because the abort works only when abortPassthrough runs outside Recovery; a test with a different chain would pass while production silently truncates. Finally, run one integration test against a real listener and assert that reading the body of a failed export ends in an error such as io.ErrUnexpectedEOF rather than a clean EOF.
sections.title: Test it the way a client reads it

readings.takeaway: Fetch the first page before writing, stream CSV page by page with csv.Writer.Flush and c.Writer.Flush, stop on the request context, build Content-Disposition with mime.FormatMediaType, prefix formula-leading cells, and abort the connection on late failures from outside gin.Recovery.
readings.title: Streaming CSV exports in Gin: keyset pages, two flushes, formula-safe cells and an abort on late failure
wrongAnswers: A 500 Internal Server Error that replaces the 200
A connection reset, because net/http aborts the response

cautions: An in-memory queue loses every job on restart.
Guessable job IDs leak other users' results without owner checks.
designGuide.cost: A job store, a worker pool with its own shutdown, polling traffic and result retention; durability adds a jobs table, leases and idempotent work.
strengths: Request latency stays small whatever the job costs.
Overload is explicit: a bounded queue and a 503 with Retry-After.

readings.hint: Look up when net/http cancels the context of an incoming server request.
readings.introduction: Some requests ask for work that takes longer than any sensible request budget: a monthly report, a re-index, a large import. Holding the connection open ties up a goroutine, a proxy slot and the client's patience, and a timeout halfway leaves the client unsure whether anything happened. The asynchronous pattern splits the work from the request: the POST validates and enqueues, answers 202 Accepted with the URL of a job resource, and the client polls that resource until it reports a result or a failure.
readings.nuance: net/http cancels an incoming request's context when ServeHTTP returns, so the job sees context.Canceled. context.WithoutCancel keeps the values and drops the cancellation; the worker then adds its own deadline.
readings.objective: Accept slow work with 202 and a job Location, bound it with a queue and a fixed worker pool, refuse overload with 503 and Retry-After, and keep jobs running after the request ends.
readings.question: A Gin handler enqueues a job that carries c.Request.Context() and returns 202. What happens to that context by the time a worker runs the job?
readings.reviewAnswer: Canceled once ServeHTTP returns; detach it

sections.body: RFC 9110 defines 202 as accepted for processing, with processing not yet complete and possibly never completing; the response ought to describe the request's current status and point to a status monitor. In practice that means three things. Everything that can be rejected synchronously is rejected before the 202: malformed input, missing permission and an exhausted quota get a 4xx immediately, because after a 202 the job resource is the only channel left. The 202 carries a Location header with the job URL; RFC 9110 defines Location for 201 and redirects, and using it with 202 is a widespread convention clients expect. And the job resource has a small, closed lifecycle: queued, running, then succeeded with a link to the result or failed with a public error message. Terminal states never change, so a client can stop polling as soon as it sees one.
sections.title: What 202 Accepted promises

sections.body: Pool owns the job records, a buffered channel as the queue and a fixed set of workers started with WaitGroup.Go. Submit records and enqueues a job in one critical section and never blocks; the handler turns its refusal into a 503. main holds jobs inside the work function with two channels: started tells main that a worker has picked a job up, and release lets one job finish. That fixes the order of every observable state without a single sleep.
sections.title: A pool with two workers and room for one more
sections.walkthrough: Job 1 starts on the first worker and job 2 on the second, so job 3 waits in the one-slot queue and the fourth POST finds it full: 503 with Retry-After and no job created, which the final 404 confirms. October fails the datetime=2006-01 rule before any job exists. The second line matters most: once ServeHTTP has returned, the request context is canceled, yet job 1 later succeeds, because its task carries context.WithoutCancel of that context. The first release frees one worker, which takes job 3 and reports through started; the next two releases let the remaining jobs finish. Shutdown closes the queue under the lock and waits for both workers, so every job is terminal before the final GETs: job 2 failed because its work returned an error, and the other two succeeded and link to their results.

sections.body: The channel capacity is the backlog you are willing to promise, and the worker count is the concurrency the downstream system can sustain; the bounded-work lesson shows how to size both. Submit uses select with a default case, so a full queue is an immediate answer rather than a blocked handler. Waiting for space would only move the queue into parked goroutines, where nothing bounds or measures it. Answer 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After so clients and SDKs know when to come back. Prefer it to 429, which says that this client exceeded its own quota, as in the rate-limiting lesson; a full queue is a statement about the service. Submit holds the mutex while it sends and records the job, so a worker cannot update a job that does not exist yet, and the close in Shutdown cannot race a send, which would panic. The counter IDs in the demo are for readability only. Real job IDs must be unguessable, and every GET must check that the caller owns the job, or /jobs/{n+1} hands one customer the report of another, as the tenant-isolation lesson warns.
sections.title: Bound the queue, fix the workers, refuse early

sections.body: net/http cancels an incoming request's context when ServeHTTP returns, a moment after the 202 is written, so a job that runs on c.Request.Context() is canceled almost as soon as it starts. context.WithoutCancel returns a context that keeps the parent's values, such as the request ID, trace span and principal set by middleware, but has no deadline, never reports an error and has a nil Done channel. The worker adds the job's own budget with WithTimeout when the job starts rather than when it is enqueued, so time spent queued does not eat it. Give the worker the request's context and plain data, never *gin.Context or c.Copy(); the engine recycles context objects, as the context-workers lesson explains. gin.Recovery protects only the handler goroutine, and a panic in a worker goroutine kills the whole process, which is why execute recovers and records the job as failed. Shutdown here drains the queue and joins the workers. In production, bound that with the shutdown budget from the server-lifecycle lesson and give running jobs a pool-level stop signal; context.AfterFunc can cancel each job's context when the pool's context is canceled.
sections.title: Detach the request context, never the gin.Context

sections.body: Every queued and running job in this pool disappears on a deploy, a crash or an out-of-memory kill, and with two replicas the one that did not accept job 1 answers 404 for it. When losing a job is unacceptable, persist it before the 202: insert the job row in the same transaction as any business change it depends on, which is the outbox pattern from the systems.outbox-inbox lesson, and let workers claim due rows with a lease. A crashed worker's lease expires and another worker runs the job again, so execution becomes at least once and the work itself must be idempotent. A context cannot be stored, so persist the values the job needs, such as the trace ID and the principal, as columns. A client that retries a POST whose 202 was lost would create a second job, so accept an Idempotency-Key as the idempotency-keys lesson describes, and delete finished jobs and their results after a published retention period.
sections.code:
// A worker claims one due job. SKIP LOCKED lets many workers poll one table.
const claim = `
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1,
       lease_until = now() + interval '5 minutes'
WHERE id = (
    SELECT id FROM jobs
    WHERE status = 'queued' OR (status = 'running' AND lease_until < now())
    ORDER BY created_at
    LIMIT 1
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id, kind, input, trace_id`

var id, kind, traceID string
var input []byte
err := db.QueryRowContext(ctx, claim).Scan(&id, &kind, &input, &traceID)
if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
	return nil // nothing due: wait for a notification or the next poll tick
}
sections.title: An in-memory pool is a model; durable jobs live in the database
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs against PostgreSQL in your own environment. The inner SELECT finds the oldest job that is queued or whose lease has expired, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers run the same statement without blocking each other or claiming the same row. The UPDATE marks it running with a five-minute lease and counts the attempt, and the trace ID comes back as data because no context survived the restart. sql.ErrNoRows means nothing is due. A job that exceeds a maximum attempt count should move to failed rather than retry forever.

sections.body: A test that sleeps and hopes a worker has started is slow on a fast machine and flaky on a loaded one. Make the work function observable instead: an unbuffered started channel proves that a worker holds a job, a release channel decides when it finishes, and Shutdown joins the workers before the final assertions. Cover the full queue and its Retry-After, validation failures that create no job, an unknown or foreign job ID, a job that returns an error, a job that panics, Submit during shutdown and a request context canceled before the worker starts. For deadlines, the synctest lesson shows how to test them without the wall clock. Run the suite with -race, because handlers and workers touch the pool at the same time. On the client side, poll with backoff and honor Retry-After, or let the client register a webhook that is called when the job reaches a terminal state; the webhook-receiver lesson covers the receiving end.
sections.title: Test the lifecycle with channels, not sleeps

readings.takeaway: Validate synchronously, enqueue without blocking, answer 202 with a Location for the job, refuse a full queue with 503 and Retry-After, run each job on context.WithoutCancel plus its own deadline, and persist jobs when losing one is unacceptable.
readings.title: Long work behind 202 Accepted in Gin: a bounded queue, fixed workers, a job resource and an honest 503
wrongAnswers: It stays live until the client closes the connection
It inherits the server's IdleTimeout as its deadline

cautions: Dedupe records must outlive the sender's retry schedule.
A 4xx for unhandled event types only causes pointless retries.
designGuide.cost: A shared secret per sender with rotation, a dedupe store with retention, a queue and workers, and monitoring of rejection rates.
strengths: Forged, altered and replayed requests never reach business code.
Duplicate deliveries are acknowledged without reprocessing.

readings.hint: Think about what the sender's HMAC was computed over, and what binding does to the request body.
readings.introduction: A webhook endpoint is a public URL that anyone can POST to, called by a sender that retries whatever it believes failed. Three things matter more than the business logic: proving the request came from the sender unaltered, refusing old requests replayed by someone who captured one, and processing each event once although it may arrive several times. The status code is an instruction to the sender's retry machinery, so choose it as carefully as the verification.
readings.nuance: Binding reads c.Request.Body to EOF, and re-encoding the struct does not reproduce the sender's bytes, so the MAC can only be checked on the raw body, read first and then restored for the handler.
readings.objective: Receive signed webhooks in Gin by authenticating the raw body before binding, rejecting replays, deduplicating deliveries and choosing status codes that make the sender retry only when a retry can help.
readings.question: Why must a Gin webhook handler verify the signature before it calls c.ShouldBindJSON?
readings.reviewAnswer: The MAC covers raw bytes; binding consumes them

sections.body: The sender computes HMAC-SHA256 with a shared secret over the exact bytes it sends; in this lesson that is the timestamp header, a dot and the body, a layout many providers use in some form, but follow your sender's documentation for the precise format. The receiver must recompute the MAC over the same bytes. Binding first breaks that: c.ShouldBindJSON reads c.Request.Body to the end, and re-encoding the bound struct does not reproduce the sender's bytes, because field order, spacing, escaping, number formatting and unknown fields all change. It also parses unauthenticated input before you know who sent it. So the verification middleware reads the body once through http.MaxBytesReader, checks it, and puts the same bytes back as a fresh reader so the handler can bind as usual. io.ReadAll is right here, unlike in the streaming-import lesson: a webhook payload is small, the cap is tight and the MAC needs every byte anyway. c.GetRawData is the same io.ReadAll with no limit of its own, so it needs the MaxBytesReader just as much.
sections.title: The signature covers bytes, so read them before anything parses them

sections.body: verifySignature runs on the /webhooks group only. It bounds and reads the body, verifies the signature and then the timestamp against an injected clock, records the precise reason with c.Error when it rejects, and restores the body. receive binds the event, acknowledges types it does not handle, and asks Inbox to deduplicate and enqueue in one step. main signs each delivery with a test-only secret, the way a sender would, and prints the status, the body and the reason an access log would record.
sections.title: A payments endpoint and seven deliveries
sections.walkthrough: The first delivery is queued with 202. The sender's retry 40 seconds later has a new timestamp and a valid signature over the same event, and Inbox answers 200 duplicate without queuing it again. Changing the amount after signing breaks the MAC; replaying a genuine delivery whose timestamp is ten minutes old passes the MAC but fails the five-minute window. Both get the same 400 body, while the log line tells them apart. An event type the service does not handle is acknowledged with 200, so the sender stops offering it. With evt_3 queued the two-slot queue is full, so evt_4 gets 503 with Retry-After and is not recorded as seen, and the sender's next attempt will be accepted. The worker starts only after the requests here, purely so that the queue-full case is deterministic; in a service it runs from startup.

sections.body: verify decodes each hex signature and compares it with hmac.Equal, which does not return at the first differing byte; the security.constant-time lesson explains why == and bytes.Equal leak how much of a guess was right. Accepting any v1= entry lets the sender sign with an old and a new secret during rotation; keep both configured on your side until the old one is retired. The timestamp is inside the MAC, so an attacker cannot refresh a captured request without the secret. It is parsed strictly and compared with the injected clock, which lets tests move time without sleeping, and the five-minute tolerance applies in both directions to absorb clock skew, so keep server clocks synchronized. The signature is checked first so that a stale-timestamp log line always describes an authentic request. Every verification failure returns the same body; the specific reason goes to the log. Not every provider signs a timestamp: GitHub's X-Hub-Signature-256 covers only the body, so replay protection there rests on deduplicating the X-GitHub-Delivery ID.
sections.title: Compare in constant time, then check the clock

sections.body: Senders deliver at least once. A timeout on their side or a lost response triggers a retry with the same event ID, usually with a new timestamp and signature, and Inbox turns it into 200 duplicate. Two orderings matter. Deduplicate only after verification, or forged requests can plant event IDs and make you drop the real events later. And mark an ID as seen in the same step that queues the event, only if queuing succeeded; otherwise a 503 is followed by a retry that is wrongly answered as a duplicate, and the event is lost. The tolerance window and the dedupe store work together: the window limits how long a captured request stays usable, dedupe covers replays inside it, and because sender retries can arrive hours or days later, dedupe records must outlive the sender's retry schedule. In a real service the inbox is a table with a unique key on sender and event ID, written in the same transaction as the job that will process the event, which is the inbox half of the systems.outbox-inbox lesson.
sections.title: Deduplicate after verification, and record only what you queued
sections.walkthrough: This fragment runs against PostgreSQL in your own environment. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes the duplicate check and the insert one atomic statement, so two concurrent deliveries of the same event cannot both pass. Zero affected rows means a duplicate, reported as duplicate=true so the handler answers 200. The job row for the workers from the async-jobs lesson goes into the same transaction, and a nil error from Commit is the only path to 202; any error before that becomes a 503, and because the rollback also removes the inbox row, a retry from the sender is processed rather than taken for a duplicate.

sections.body: The handler verifies, deduplicates, enqueues and answers; the business work happens later in a worker. Senders time out quickly, and GitHub, for example, expects a response within 10 seconds, so processing inline turns every slow database moment into a retry of an event you may already have handled. Treat the status code as an instruction to the sender's retry logic. 2xx means do not send this again: 202 for a queued event, 200 for a duplicate, and 200 for an event type you do not handle, because a 4xx there only causes retries and, with some senders, a disabled endpoint. 4xx means retrying the same bytes cannot help: a bad or missing signature, a stale timestamp, malformed JSON in an authentic body, or a payload over the cap, which gets 413. 5xx means the failure is yours and temporary: a full queue or an unavailable database gets 503 with Retry-After, and an unexpected panic becomes a 500 through Recovery. Senders differ: many retry any non-2xx with backoff, some never retry, some ignore Retry-After, and several disable an endpoint after a run of failures. These codes are truthful under every policy; check which codes your sender treats specially, and alert on a rising 4xx rate, which usually means a rotated secret or a drifting clock.
sections.title: Answer in milliseconds, with a status that steers retries

sections.body: Build test deliveries with the same sign function and a test-only secret, as main does, and never commit a real one. Cover a valid delivery, a retry, a tampered body, a tampered timestamp header, missing headers, malformed hex, a wrong secret, two signatures during rotation, timestamps exactly at the tolerance and one second beyond in both directions, a body over the cap, malformed JSON with a valid signature, an unhandled type, and a full queue followed by a successful retry. Assert that every rejected delivery leaves the inbox unchanged. Add a route-table test that fails if a webhook route is registered outside the verifying group, and remember that a webhook route has no browser session: exempt it from CSRF middleware, never from signature verification.
sections.title: Test with signed fixtures and a fake clock

readings.takeaway: Read the bounded raw body once, verify an HMAC over timestamp and body with hmac.Equal, reject timestamps outside a window from an injected clock, dedupe by event ID only after verification, enqueue and answer 2xx fast, and keep 5xx for failures a retry can fix.
readings.title: Signed webhooks in Gin: verify the raw bytes, reject stale timestamps, dedupe event IDs, answer fast
wrongAnswers: Binding removes the signature header from the request
ShouldBindJSON rejects bodies longer than the HMAC block

cautions: A new client or Transport per request defeats connection reuse.
Forwarding upstream bodies or headers leaks internal details.
LimitReader alone truncates silently; read the limit plus one byte.
designGuide.cost: One client constructor, an error-mapping function and a fake RoundTripper for tests; tuning pool sizes and timeouts needs load tests against the real upstream.
strengths: Upstream failures become stable, documented error codes.
A hung upstream costs one bounded budget, not a stuck goroutine.

readings.hint: The slow party is neither your client nor your own code.
readings.introduction: Most Gin services are also HTTP clients: they call a payment provider, an inventory service or a search cluster while their own caller waits. Every such call borrows the caller's time, a pooled connection and memory for the reply. Done naively, one slow or misbehaving upstream turns into piled-up goroutines, exhausted sockets and error responses that quote another team's database errors to your users.
readings.nuance: 504 says a server acting as a gateway got no timely answer from an upstream. 408 would blame the client for sending its request slowly, and the Go error text would leak internal hostnames.
readings.objective: Call an upstream HTTP API from a Gin handler through a shared, budgeted http.Client and map every failure to your own 404, 502 or 504 without leaking upstream details.
readings.question: A Gin handler's call to an upstream API exceeds its per-call context deadline. What should the handler return to its own client?
readings.reviewAnswer: 504 Gateway Timeout, in your own error format

sections.body: http.Get uses http.DefaultClient, which has no overall Timeout. DefaultTransport bounds dialing and the TLS handshake but sets no ResponseHeaderTimeout, so an upstream that accepts the connection and never answers holds the handler goroutine until something cancels it, and nothing will unless the request carries a context. Building a new http.Client with a new Transport per request is the opposite mistake: every Transport owns its own connection pool, so keep-alive never helps and idle sockets pile up. io.ReadAll on the body trusts the upstream to be small. Copying the upstream status and body into c.Data turns their 500 into yours and their SQL error into your public API. The fix is four rules: one client built at startup, a per-call context derived from the request, a cap on the bytes you read, and an explicit mapping from upstream outcomes to your own responses.
sections.title: What goes wrong with http.Get inside a handler

sections.body: The Transport owns connections, so it is where the phase timeouts live: dialing, the TLS handshake and the wait for response headers. Client.Timeout covers the whole exchange including the body and acts as a backstop. Construct the client in the composition root described in the config-startup lesson and inject it into the handler struct, so a test can swap the Transport without touching the handler.
sections.title: Build the client once, with budgets on the Transport
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own native environment; it dials real hosts. ForceAttemptHTTP2 matters because the Transport documentation says a custom DialContext or TLS config disables HTTP/2 unless it is set. ResponseHeaderTimeout counts from the moment the request is fully written until headers arrive; it does not cover reading the body. MaxIdleConnsPerHost defaults to http.DefaultMaxIdleConnsPerHost, which is 2, so a busy service closes and reopens connections constantly without a higher value. MaxConnsPerHost makes excess requests queue for a connection, and that queueing time still counts against each request's context. CheckRedirect returning http.ErrUseLastResponse makes Do return the 3xx response unfollowed; the SSRF lesson in the security course explains why following redirects needs its own policy.

sections.body: The program wires an Inventory client into a Gin route. Stock derives a 50 ms budget from c.Request.Context(), builds the request with http.NewRequestWithContext, sends this service's own token and reads at most 64 KiB. The upstream is a fake http.RoundTripper, the interface the real Transport implements, so the genuine http.Client code path runs without a socket. Seven SKUs exercise success, a missing item, an upstream 500 with internal headers, an oversized body, a refused connection, a hung upstream and a client that disconnected first.
sections.title: Pass the request context, cap the body, translate the result
sections.walkthrough: The A-1 line shows what the upstream received: a deadline on the context, the service token, and no trace of the caller's Authorization or Cookie headers. NOPE maps the upstream 404 to the domain error errUnknownSKU and then to this API's own 404. ERR proves nothing leaks: the client sees inventory_unavailable while the status goes to the log, and X-Backend-Host and the pq: text stay behind. BIG reads 64 KiB plus one byte, sees the extra byte and refuses, instead of decoding a silently truncated document. DOWN and SLOW both fail inside Client.Do, and errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) separates the timeout (504) from the refused connection (502). For GONE the request context is already canceled; fail records 499, the nginx convention for a client that closed the request, purely for logs and metrics.

sections.body: RFC 9110 defines 502 Bad Gateway as an invalid response from an upstream and 504 Gateway Timeout as no timely response. Use 502 for refused connections, upstream 5xx, unreadable, oversized or malformed bodies, and 504 when your per-call budget expires. errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) also catches an expired Client.Timeout, because in the Go 1.27 source the timeout error net/http returns has an Is method that matches context.DeadlineExceeded. An upstream 404 for a SKU is a domain fact, so it becomes your 404 with your error code. An upstream 400, 401 or 403 usually means your service built a bad request or holds a wrong credential: that is your bug, so answer 502 and alert, and never pass a 401 through, or the client will think its own login failed. Never echo the upstream body, its Set-Cookie, Server or routing headers, or its status text; the problem-details lesson defines the envelope to use instead. And do not forward the caller's Authorization or Cookie: the upstream would act with the user's authority and log their credentials. Send a service credential and pass the user's identity as data when the upstream needs it.
sections.title: Status codes are yours: 502, 504, 404 and the client that left

sections.body: io.LimitReader alone truncates silently, so read MaxBody+1 bytes and treat a longer result as a failure. When you do not set Accept-Encoding yourself, the Transport asks for gzip and decompresses transparently, which means the limit applies to decoded bytes, the number that protects your memory; if you set the header yourself, you must decompress and bound the result yourself, as the compression lesson in this unit does for request bodies. Always close the body, and remember that an HTTP/1.1 connection returns to the pool only when its body was read to EOF: drain a few kilobytes on error paths and let anything larger close the connection. Decode into a struct holding only the fields you use. encoding/json ignores unknown fields, so the upstream can add warehouse or cost_cents without breaking you, and those fields never reach your clients because your type does not have them. If a proxy in front of the upstream sometimes returns HTML error pages, check the Content-Type before decoding.
sections.title: Read the body deliberately: limits, draining and tolerant decoding

sections.body: A fake RoundTripper records each outgoing request and returns scripted responses or errors, including one that blocks on the request context to model a hung upstream. Assert the method, the escaped path, the headers you send and the ones you must not forward, and that a deadline is present. Each row of your error mapping becomes one test case, exactly as the program's seven SKUs do. Keep one integration test against a real server, httptest.NewServer or a staging upstream, run in your own environment, for what only a real Transport shows: dial and header timeouts, TLS, HTTP/2 and connection reuse. In production, count upstream calls by outcome (ok, not_found, 5xx, timeout, too_large) next to a latency histogram per upstream, so a spike of 502s says which dependency failed and how; the metrics lesson shows how to keep those labels bounded.
sections.title: Test the client at the RoundTripper seam

readings.takeaway: Build one http.Client with Transport timeouts at startup, derive each call's context from c.Request.Context(), read at most a fixed number of bytes, and translate every upstream outcome into your own 404, 502 or 504 without forwarding their bodies, their headers or your caller's credentials.
readings.title: Upstream calls from Gin: one shared client, the request deadline, a bounded body and your own error codes
wrongAnswers: 408 Request Timeout, since the request took too long
500 Internal Server Error with the Go error text

cautions: Retries at several layers multiply load; retry at one.
Count only transport errors and 5xx as breaker failures.
A request body must be replayable through GetBody to retry it.
designGuide.cost: A few hundred lines of policy code or a reviewed library, per-upstream state, and metrics for attempts, budget refusals and breaker transitions; thresholds need tuning against real traffic.
strengths: Transient blips are absorbed before the client notices.
An outage gets fast 503s instead of queued, doomed attempts.

readings.hint: Ask what happens if the first attempt actually committed.
readings.introduction: A retry turns a transient failure into a success and a persistent failure into extra load at the worst possible moment. Whether a retry helps depends on three questions: is it safe to send the request twice, is the failure likely to clear soon, and how much extra traffic is the fleet already sending. This lesson builds the client side of those answers behind a Gin handler, with a seeded random source and an injected clock so every wait is reproducible.
readings.nuance: A timeout is ambiguous: the first attempt may have succeeded and only its response was lost. Resending the same Idempotency-Key lets the upstream replay the stored result instead of charging twice; PUT and DELETE are idempotent too.
readings.objective: Wrap upstream calls in a retry policy that respects idempotency, Retry-After and a shared budget, and use a circuit breaker so Gin answers 503 quickly while a dependency is down.
readings.question: A POST to a payment upstream times out after the request was fully sent. When may the client retry it automatically?
readings.reviewAnswer: Only if the upstream honors an Idempotency-Key you resend
readings.reviewPrompt: Retry a POST after a timeout?

sections.body: RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE as idempotent: sending one twice has the same intended effect as sending it once. POST and PATCH are not, and a timeout is ambiguous, because the first attempt may have committed and only the response was lost. Retrying such a request can create a second order or a second charge. A client may retry a POST only when the upstream honors an Idempotency-Key and the client resends the same key on every attempt; the idempotency-keys lesson builds that server side. Worth retrying: connection errors, 502, 503, 504 and 429. Not worth retrying: other 4xx, which will fail again identically, and usually 500, which is often a deterministic bug. Retry at one layer only, ideally the one closest to the failing dependency; the cache-stampede lesson in the Go course shows how retries stacked at several layers multiply load.
sections.title: Which requests and which failures may be retried

sections.body: The upstream is a scripted RoundTripper, and the injected clock's Sleep only advances time, so the program runs in milliseconds and prints the same waits on every run. Jitter comes from math/rand/v2 with fixed PCG seeds. Eight client requests walk through a flaky success, a POST without and with an Idempotency-Key, upstream throttling with Retry-After, an outage that first empties the retry budget and then opens the breaker, a request rejected while the breaker is open, and the half-open probe that closes it.
sections.title: Backoff, Retry-After, a budget and a breaker in one client
sections.walkthrough: Do deposits into the budget once per call, then loops. Each attempt first asks the breaker, refreshes the body through GetBody, sends, and records success or failure; only transport errors and 5xx count against the breaker, so the 429 does not. A non-retryable status returns at once. Otherwise the wait is the jittered backoff, replaced by Retry-After when the upstream sends one, and the switch names the first reason to stop: unsafe method, attempts used, breaker now open, wait past the deadline, or no budget. The first outage request spends the last whole token on one retry and then finds the budget empty; the second takes the third consecutive failure, which opens the breaker. The next request never reaches the upstream, and respond turns OpenError into 503 with Retry-After rounded up to whole seconds. After 31 simulated seconds one probe succeeds and the breaker closes. trace exists only to print attempts and is not safe for concurrent use; a real client would emit metrics instead.

sections.body: Clients that failed together and back off by the same schedule retry together, in synchronized waves that knock the recovering upstream over again. Full jitter draws each wait uniformly from zero to min(Cap, Base times 2 to the power of the attempt number minus one): the ceiling grows exponentially while individual waits spread across it, and the cap keeps the exponent from producing minute-long waits. In production every process should draw differently, which math/rand/v2's top-level functions already do because they are randomly seeded; in tests inject a *rand.Rand built from rand.NewPCG with fixed seeds, which yields the same sequence every run. Time works the same way: depend on a clock interface, give tests a fake one, and give production a sleep that also watches the request context, as in the fragment below. Retry-After, defined in RFC 9110 section 10.2.3, may hold seconds or an HTTP-date; prefer it over your own guess, but a value longer than the remaining budget means give up now and tell your own client when to return.
sections.title: Jitter spreads the herd; seeds and clocks make it testable
sections.walkthrough: This fragment is the production counterpart of fakeClock and runs in your own native environment. It refuses a wait that would end after the context deadline, because a retry that starts after the caller gave up is pure waste. time.NewTimer with a deferred Stop releases the timer when the request is canceled first, and the select returns ctx.Err() so the retry loop stops instead of sending another attempt for a client that has already left.

sections.body: MaxAttempts bounds one call, not the fleet. When every request fails, three attempts each triple the load on a dependency that may be failing precisely because it is overloaded. A budget ties retries to overall traffic: every call deposits Ratio tokens, every retry spends one, and the balance is capped, so over time retries add at most Ratio times the request rate. Google's SRE book describes the same idea as a per-client retry budget of about ten percent; the program uses 0.5 only so that the effect appears within eight requests. Keep one budget per upstream in each process; coordinating budgets across instances is rarely worth the complexity. Export the number of retries and of budget refusals as metrics: a sudden rise in refusals is an early, cheap signal that a dependency is degrading.
sections.title: A retry budget caps amplification across requests

sections.body: Closed: calls pass and consecutive failures are counted; at the threshold the breaker opens. Open: calls fail immediately with no socket and no waiting, which protects both the upstream and your own goroutines. After the cooldown the breaker turns half-open and lets exactly one probe through; success closes it, failure reopens it for a fresh cooldown, and other callers are refused while the probe is in flight. Allow and Record take a mutex because every request touches them concurrently. While open, the handler chose not to do the work, so it answers 503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After set to the remaining cooldown, in your own error format, consistent with the timeouts lesson's convention; if the product allows, serve a stale cached value instead. Keep one breaker per upstream, or per endpoint when endpoints fail independently, never one for everything. Consecutive failures are the simplest trigger; production breakers often use a failure rate over a sliding window with a minimum request volume, so two failures in a quiet hour do not trip it.
sections.title: Breaker states and what the Gin handler returns while open

sections.body: Each test row is a method, an optional Idempotency-Key, an upstream script and the expected attempts, waits, final status and breaker state; with an injected clock and seeded random source the assertions can be exact. Add a concurrency test in which many goroutines hit a half-open breaker and exactly one RoundTrip call happens. Check that every attempt resends the body: http.NewRequest sets GetBody only for *bytes.Buffer, *bytes.Reader and *strings.Reader bodies, so for any other reader GetBody is nil and safeToRetry refuses rather than sending an empty second attempt. In staging, inject faults by making a test upstream return 503 or hang, and watch the attempt counts, budget refusals and breaker transitions on your dashboards before a real outage does it for you.
sections.title: Test the policy as a table of scripts

readings.takeaway: Retry only idempotent requests or those carrying an Idempotency-Key, only on transient failures, with capped full-jitter backoff, honored Retry-After and a shared retry budget, and put a per-upstream circuit breaker in front so an outage gets fast 503s with Retry-After instead of more load.
readings.title: Retrying upstream calls from Gin: only when safe, jittered backoff, a retry budget and a circuit breaker
wrongAnswers: Always, since a timeout means the upstream never got it
Never, because only GET requests can be retried safely

cautions: Never compress SSE, ranges, images or already-encoded bodies.
Bound decompressed request bodies, not just the wire bytes.
A reverse proxy or CDN usually compresses better than the app.
designGuide.cost: CPU on every compressible response, a small buffer per request, and a wrapper whose every write path must stay in sync with gin.ResponseWriter as Gin evolves.
strengths: Text APIs typically shrink several times on slow links.
A per-route opt-out keeps BREACH-prone pages uncompressed.

readings.hint: The cache needs to know which request header changed the response.
readings.introduction: JSON, CSV and HTML often shrink several times under gzip, which matters on mobile links and metered egress. A compression middleware sits between every handler and the network, so its bugs appear everywhere at once: a missing Vary header serves gzip to a client that cannot read it, a stale Content-Length truncates bodies, a compressed event stream stalls, and a page that mixes a secret with reflected input becomes a BREACH oracle.
readings.nuance: Vary tells caches to key the stored response by Accept-Encoding. Without it on both variants, the first stored copy is served to every client regardless of what it can decode; no-transform only forbids intermediaries from changing the body.
readings.objective: Write a gzip middleware for Gin that negotiates Accept-Encoding correctly and skips responses that must not be compressed, and accept gzip request bodies without a decompression-bomb hole.
readings.question: A gzip middleware compresses responses for clients that send Accept-Encoding: gzip. Which header stops a shared cache from serving the compressed bytes to a client that cannot decode them?
readings.reviewAnswer: Vary: Accept-Encoding, on gzip and identity responses

sections.body: Accept-Encoding is a list of content codings with optional weights. "gzip, br" accepts both; "gzip;q=0, br" explicitly refuses gzip; "*;q=0.5" accepts any coding not listed. An explicit entry beats the wildcard, q=0 means not acceptable, and several Accept-Encoding header lines form one list, which is why the code joins Header.Values. RFC 9110 lets a server pick any coding when the header is absent, but clients that omit it are usually simple tools, so identity is the safe answer. The client's preference is only half the decision. The other half depends on the response: its status, its Content-Type, its size, whether a Content-Encoding is already set and whether the handler streams. None of that is known before the handler writes, so the wrapper buffers the first bytes and decides at the last possible moment.
sections.title: Negotiate with q-values, then decide per response

sections.body: Compress swaps c.Writer for a gzipWriter that embeds the original gin.ResponseWriter. decide runs exactly once: when buffered bytes reach 512, on Flush or WriteHeaderNow, or after the chain returns. NoCompression lets one handler opt out, and GunzipBody accepts compressed uploads. main sends twelve requests and decodes every gzip response, so a corrupt stream would show up as an error line.
sections.title: A gzip writer around gin.ResponseWriter
sections.walkthrough: Overriding Write is not enough. gin.ResponseWriter also has WriteString, which io.WriteString and Gin's renderers can reach, and an embedded method would send bytes straight past gzip; WriteHeaderNow is what c.Render calls for 204 and 304 and what AbortWithStatus calls. Status works through the embedded writer because Gin's WriteHeader only records the code until the first real write. finish runs after c.Next and before Gin's engine flushes its own writer, and gz.Close writes the gzip trailer. Unwrap lets http.ResponseController reach SetWriteDeadline, while its Flush finds the wrapper's Flush first, because ResponseController checks for a Flusher before unwrapping. Writers come from a sync.Pool because each gzip.Writer carries sizeable compressor state. In the output, gzip;q=0 and the missing header get identity, *;q=0.5 gets gzip, the 304 carries Vary and no body, and the PNG, the event stream and the opted-out page pass through untouched.

sections.body: Add Vary: Accept-Encoding to every response whose encoding depends on that header, including the identity ones; otherwise a shared cache that stored the gzip variant serves it to a client that sent no Accept-Encoding. A 304 must repeat the Vary its 200 would carry. Delete Content-Length, which described the uncompressed bytes. A strong ETag names exact bytes, as the conditional-requests lesson explains, so weaken it as nginx does or compute one per coding; the handler's If-None-Match check uses the weak comparison, so W/"r1" still revalidates. Drop Accept-Ranges, because ranges would address the compressed stream. Skip HEAD, which has no body; 1xx, 204 and 304; 206 partial content; bodies that already have a Content-Encoding, such as precompressed assets; and every type outside the allow-list. PNG, JPEG, ZIP, video and WOFF2 are already compressed, so gzip burns CPU and can even grow them. Never compress text/event-stream: the compressor holds bytes until a block fills and proxies may buffer further, which delays the events and heartbeats the SSE lesson relies on. Below roughly half a kilobyte, gzip framing and CPU cost more than they save.
sections.title: Headers that must change with the body

sections.body: DEFLATE can shrink a run of zeros by about a thousand to one: the program's 8 MiB of zeros fits in well under 64 KiB of gzip. A limit on Content-Length or on wire bytes therefore says nothing about memory. GunzipBody applies http.MaxBytesReader twice, once to the compressed stream and once to the decompressed stream; it can wrap the *gzip.Reader because that type has a Close method. When the decoded limit trips, the handler sees *http.MaxBytesError and answers 413. One v1.12.0 surprise: MaxBytesReader asks net/http to close the connection through an unexported method that only the server's own ResponseWriter has, and Gin's writer does not forward it, so passing c.Writer loses that signal; the server still discards at most 256 KiB of unread body after the handler and closes the connection when more remains. The middleware removes Content-Encoding and sets ContentLength to -1, so later binding code does not trust values that described the compressed bytes. A coding you do not support gets 415 with an Accept-Encoding response header naming what does work, as RFC 7694 describes. gzip.Reader reads concatenated members as one stream by default, and the decoded limit still holds across them. Apply the same rule wherever you decompress yourself: upstream responses when you set Accept-Encoding manually, and archives, whose zip-slip half the path-traversal lesson covers.
sections.title: Decompression bombs: bound the bytes after gunzip

sections.body: BREACH needs four things: HTTP compression, a secret such as a CSRF token in the body, attacker-controlled input reflected into the same body, and an attacker who can make the victim's browser send many requests and observe the encrypted response sizes. Guesses that match the secret compress better, so the response gets shorter, and the secret is recovered byte by byte despite TLS. Defenses: turn compression off for such pages, as NoCompression does for the account page; mask the token with a fresh random pad per response so its bytes never repeat; keep secrets out of bodies that echo input; and limit cross-site request driving with SameSite cookies and the Sec-Fetch-Site checks from the CSRF lesson. When nginx, Envoy, a load balancer or a CDN sits in front of the service, let it compress: it offers brotli and zstd, caches compressed variants and keeps the CPU off your application. Compress in the app only when nothing in front can, and never in both places.
sections.title: BREACH, and when the proxy should compress instead
sections.walkthrough: This nginx configuration is an illustration for your own deployment, not part of the Go program. gzip_vary on adds Vary: Accept-Encoding, gzip_proxied any keeps compressing when the request itself arrived through another proxy such as a CDN, which nginx detects from the Via header, and gzip_types is an allow-list just like compressible. The /events location turns off both proxy buffering and gzip, so Server-Sent Events leave the proxy as soon as the Gin handler flushes them. With this in place, remove Compress from the Gin engine rather than running both.

readings.takeaway: Compress only allow-listed, non-streaming bodies big enough to benefit, add Vary: Accept-Encoding and drop Content-Length when you do, bound gzip request bodies after decompression, and switch compression off for pages that mix secrets with reflected input.
readings.title: Gzip in Gin by hand: negotiate q-values, wrap the writer, add Vary and know what never to compress
wrongAnswers: Content-Length set to the size of the compressed body
Cache-Control: no-transform on the gzip response

cautions: c.File follows symlinks and lists directories; never pass user paths.
If-Range needs a strong ETag, or resumes restart from zero.
Gin's FileAttachment encodes spaces as + in filename*.
designGuide.cost: A metadata lookup per download and a stored strong validator per file; very large files also need their own write deadline or offloading to object storage.
strengths: Resumable, parallel and conditional downloads come from the stdlib.
Filenames with quotes and non-ASCII letters encode correctly.

readings.hint: If-Range compares validators the strict way.
readings.introduction: A download endpoint looks like one line, c.File(path), and that line hides most of the behavior: byte ranges for resumed and parallel downloads, conditional requests, HEAD, the content type and the filename the browser saves. Knowing what Gin delegates to net/http and what it adds decides whether a large export resumes after a dropped connection or starts over, and whether a user-chosen filename can break the response header.
readings.nuance: If-Range requires the strong comparison, which a weak ETag never passes. ServeContent then ignores the Range header and sends the whole file with 200, so every resume starts again from byte zero.
readings.objective: Serve downloadable files from Gin with correct Range, If-Range, ETag and HEAD behavior, a Content-Disposition built by mime.FormatMediaType and file access confined to an os.Root.
readings.question: A client resumes with Range: bytes=1000- and If-Range: W/"v3", and the handler set ETag: W/"v3" before calling http.ServeContent. What does the client receive?
readings.reviewAnswer: Never matches, so the full file comes back with 200

sections.body: In Gin v1.12.0, c.File(path) is one line: http.ServeFile(c.Writer, c.Request, path). c.FileAttachment(path, name) sets Content-Disposition and then makes the same call, and c.FileFromFS temporarily rewrites c.Request.URL.Path and runs http.FileServer. ServeFile opens the path through http.Dir, which, as its documentation warns, follows symlinks out of the directory and serves dotfiles such as .git. It rejects requests whose URL path contains a .. element with 400, redirects URL paths ending in /index.html, lists directories and sets Last-Modified but no ETag. All three paths end in the same serveContent code, so Range, If-Range, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since and HEAD work everywhere. http.ServeContent(w, r, name, modtime, content) is the level below: you pass an io.ReadSeeker and a modification time, name is used only to guess a type, and an ETag takes part only if you set the header before the call. That makes ServeContent the right tool when files are looked up by ID, opened through os.Root or an embedded file system, or need a validator you control.
sections.title: c.File, c.FileAttachment and http.ServeContent, read from the source

sections.body: The handler maps an export ID to a server-chosen path and a display name, opens the file through an fs.FS, checks that it is a regular, seekable file, sets Content-Type, Content-Disposition, ETag and Cache-Control, and hands over to ServeContent. An in-memory fstest.MapFS plays the file system. main sends ten requests, then compares the header Gin's FileAttachment builds with mime.FormatMediaType, using a temporary file because FileAttachment only accepts a path.
sections.title: Serve by ID through ServeContent
sections.walkthrough: The full GET advertises Accept-Ranges: bytes and derives Last-Modified from the MapFile ModTime. HEAD reports the same Content-Length while ServeContent skips the body, but only because the route is registered for both methods: Gin does not send HEAD to a GET handler, it answers 404. bytes=0-9 returns 206 with Content-Range: bytes 0-9/63, and the suffix form bytes=-9 returns the last nine bytes. Two ranges produce multipart/byteranges with a random boundary, so the program prints only the media type. A range past the end gives 416 with Content-Range: bytes */63, and the ETag is gone: since Go 1.23, ServeContent's error path deletes ETag, Last-Modified, Cache-Control and Content-Encoding, unless GODEBUG=httpservecontentkeepheaders=1. If-Range with the current ETag honors the range; with a stale one the client gets the whole new file. If-None-Match yields 304. The last four lines compare the two header builders: they agree on the ASCII name, but for the non-ASCII one Gin encodes the space as + in filename* while FormatMediaType writes %20.

sections.body: A client resuming a download sends Range: bytes=N- together with If-Range carrying the ETag or Last-Modified of the copy it holds. If the file changed in between, it must receive the whole new file, not bytes of a new version spliced onto an old prefix. ServeContent compares If-Range strongly: a weak ETag such as W/"v3" never matches, so every resume silently restarts from zero, and a date matches only to the second. Store a strong validator with the file, a version number or a content hash computed once at write time; hashing a large file on every request is far too expensive. The Go 1.27 source adds defensive rules worth knowing: a range starting beyond the end is a 416 except for empty files, which get 200; ranges whose sizes add up to more than the file are ignored and answered with 200, which defeats overlapping-range amplification; and a header with more than 200 ranges is ignored. Never compress a ServeContent response: ranges address identity bytes, and the source comments that it omits Content-Length when you set Content-Encoding because that combination is already wrong.
sections.title: Range and If-Range depend on a strong validator
