sections.body: The name a user sees is display data. It contains spaces, quotes and non-ASCII letters, and when users choose it, semicolons, control characters and very long strings too. Concatenation produces headers that parse wrongly: an unescaped quote ends the parameter early and a semicolon starts a new one. mime.FormatMediaType("attachment", map[string]string{"filename": name}) writes a bare token when it can, a quoted string with backslash escapes for ASCII with spaces or quotes, and RFC 2231 percent-encoding in filename* when the name contains non-ASCII or control characters; it returns an empty string for an invalid type or parameter name, so check for that. Gin's FileAttachment escapes quotes for ASCII names but uses url.QueryEscape otherwise, which turns spaces into +, and browsers decode filename* by RFC 8187, where + is a literal plus. RFC 6266 suggests an ASCII filename fallback next to filename* for old clients; FormatMediaType cannot emit both from one map, so add it yourself if you need it. Set an explicit Content-Type and nosniff, as the security-headers lesson recommends, so an HTML file is never rendered inline from your origin.
sections.title: Build Content-Disposition, never concatenate it

sections.body: The handler takes an fs.FS, so production passes root.FS() for an os.Root opened once at startup, and every name then resolves beneath that directory; the path-traversal lesson in the security course explains what os.Root guarantees and what it does not. Look files up by ID after an authorization check, keep the storage path and display name in your database, and never let a client name a path. Large files collide with http.Server.WriteTimeout, which the server-lifecycle lesson describes as one deadline for the entire response: a 2 GB export on a slow link needs its own deadline through http.ResponseController, sized to the file, or a separate download server. For heavy traffic, redirect to a signed object-storage URL or let the proxy send the file. Test with a table of Range, If-Range, If-None-Match and HEAD requests through ServeHTTP, assert byte-exact 206 bodies and the 416 Content-Range, and feed hostile filenames with quotes, semicolons, CR LF and non-ASCII letters into the header builder.
sections.title: Open through os.Root at startup and keep large files in budget
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in your composition root and runs in your own native environment against a real directory. os.OpenRoot fails early if the directory is missing, which is better than a 404 on the first download. root.FS() returns an fs.FS whose files are *os.File values, so the seekability check in download passes and ServeContent can serve ranges. The commented line shows where a per-response write deadline goes for very large files; budgetFor is your own policy function.

readings.takeaway: Look files up by ID, open them through os.Root, set Content-Type, a strong ETag and a Content-Disposition from mime.FormatMediaType, then let http.ServeContent handle Range, If-Range, conditional requests and HEAD, and never compress the result.
readings.title: File downloads in Gin: ServeContent for ranges and validators, a safe Content-Disposition, files opened by ID
wrongAnswers: 206 Partial Content starting at byte 1000
412 Precondition Failed, because the tag is weak

cautions: Gin's NegotiateFormat ignores q-values and letter case.
c.Negotiate has no CSV branch and answers 406 with no body.
Vary: Accept fragments shared caches; prefer ?format= for links.
designGuide.cost: A small negotiation function with its tests, one renderer per representation, and lower CDN hit ratios on URLs that vary on Accept.
strengths: One URL serves API clients, spreadsheets and browsers.
q-aware matching returns what clients actually asked for.

readings.hint: Look at what parseAccept keeps from each element of the header.
readings.introduction: Content negotiation lets one URL return the representation each client prefers: JSON for an API client, CSV for a spreadsheet import, HTML for a browser. Gin offers c.NegotiateFormat and c.Negotiate for this, and reading their v1.12.0 source shows that they implement much less of the HTTP rules than their names suggest. The gaps are easy to close, but only once you know where they are.
readings.nuance: parseAccept cuts every element at its first semicolon, so q=0 disappears and text/csv is the first accepted entry that matches an offer. RFC 9110 would exclude it and pick application/json through */*.
readings.objective: Serve JSON, CSV and HTML from one Gin handler with q-value-aware negotiation, a 406 that lists what is available, Vary: Accept for caches and a ?format= override where URLs must name the representation.
readings.question: A client sends Accept: text/csv;q=0, */* and a Gin v1.12.0 handler calls c.NegotiateFormat("application/json", "text/csv"). What does it return?
readings.reviewAnswer: text/csv, because Gin discards q-values

sections.body: parseAccept splits the header on commas, cuts each element at its first semicolon and trims spaces, so q-values and every other parameter are thrown away. NegotiateFormat caches that list in c.Accepted, which SetAccepted can replace, returns your first offer when the header is missing or empty, and panics if you pass no offers. Otherwise it walks the accepted entries in the client's order and compares each with your offers byte by byte: a * at the same position in either string matches the rest, and an accepted entry that is a prefix of an offer also matches, so even Accept: a selects application/json. Three consequences follow. Header order beats q: "application/json;q=0.1, text/csv" gets JSON. q=0 counts as acceptance: "text/csv;q=0, */*" gets CSV, the one type the client excluded. And media types compare case-sensitively although RFC 9110 says they are case-insensitive, so "Application/JSON" matches nothing. c.Negotiate switches on that result for JSON, HTML, XML, YAML, TOML, ProtoBuf and BSON; any other offer, including text/csv and even text/xml, falls to the default branch, AbortWithError with 406, which commits the status with an empty body.
sections.title: How Gin matches Accept, read from the source

sections.body: negotiate implements RFC 9110 section 12.5.1: each offer takes the q-value of the most specific media range that matches it, an exact type beating type/* and type/* beating */*, q=0 excludes, the highest q wins and ties go to the server's order. The program prints Gin's choice and the RFC choice side by side for seven Accept headers, then sends seven requests through the real router, including a ?format= override and a call to c.Negotiate.
sections.title: One handler, three representations, two negotiators
sections.walkthrough: ginChoice builds a fresh test context per header because NegotiateFormat caches the parsed list in c.Accepted. The table shows the three divergences described above; the browser header agrees in both because text/html comes first and has the highest q. In report, a format query parameter is checked against an allow-list and, when present, replaces negotiation entirely, so no Vary is sent. Without it the handler sets Vary: Accept before choosing, so even the 406 carries it. CSV is rendered with encoding/csv into a buffer and sent with c.Data; HTML uses the template installed with SetHTMLTemplate. image/png gets a 406 whose JSON body lists the available types. ?format=xml is a 400, because the URL itself is wrong. The last line is c.Negotiate offered text/csv and asked for text/csv: 406 with no body and no Content-Type, since it has no CSV renderer.

sections.body: An empty result means none of your representations is acceptable. Answer 406 Not Acceptable with a body listing what is available, as RFC 9110 suggests, written in your normal error format; a client that accepts only image/png will receive something it did not ask for either way. RFC 9110 also allows ignoring Accept and sending a default instead. Choose one behavior and document it, though for API clients 406 is kinder, because silent JSON delivered to a CSV importer fails later and more confusingly. A missing Accept means anything is acceptable, so put the safest default first in the offers. Browsers send text/html first with */*;q=0.8, so a person opening the URL gets HTML. Send Vary: Accept on every negotiated response so caches know the URL has several representations; without it, a CDN that stored the CSV serves it to the next JSON client. The price is fragmentation: every distinct Accept string becomes its own cache key, and many caches do not normalize it. Each representation also needs its own ETag, as the conditional-requests lesson requires.
sections.title: 406, defaults and Vary: Accept

sections.body: Negotiation hides the representation in a header, and sometimes it belongs in the URL. A "Download CSV" link in a page or an email cannot set Accept, and a browser's address bar always sends its own. A CDN keys on the URL without needing Vary, and logs and support tickets show exactly what was requested. So many APIs accept ?format=csv, or a suffix such as /sales.csv, as an explicit override validated against an allow-list, and fall back to Accept only when it is absent. An unknown value is a 400 because the URL is wrong; 406 is about the Accept header. Never copy the query value into Content-Type, or ?format=text/html turns your JSON into a page a browser renders, which is reflected XSS. CSV has a hazard of its own: a cell beginning with =, +, - or @ is evaluated as a formula when a user opens the export in a spreadsheet, so prefix such values with a single quote when people will open the file, as OWASP's CSV injection page describes.
sections.title: When ?format= beats the Accept header

sections.body: Turn the comparison table into a test against your real router. Include a missing header, curl's */*, a browser's full header, q=0 exclusions, a low q listed first, letter-case variants and a type you do not offer. Assert the status, the media type parsed from Content-Type and Vary: Accept, and decode each body with the matching reader, encoding/json for JSON and encoding/csv for CSV, so a renderer that writes the wrong format with the right header cannot pass. Add cases for ?format=: a valid override with no Vary, and 400 for an unknown value.
sections.title: Test every Accept header you claim to support
sections.walkthrough: This test fragment lives in your service package and runs with go test in your own project; newRouter is the constructor from the first lesson's pattern. Each row names an Accept header and the status and media type you promise for it. mime.ParseMediaType strips the charset parameter so the comparison is about the type alone. The q-value rows and the TEXT/HTML row fail with Gin's NegotiateFormat and pass with the q-aware negotiate function, which is exactly the regression this test exists to catch.

readings.takeaway: Treat Gin's NegotiateFormat as a first-match helper that ignores q-values and letter case, negotiate by q yourself when clients depend on it, answer 406 in your own format, send Vary: Accept on every negotiated response and offer ?format= where URLs must name the representation.
readings.title: Content negotiation in Gin: what NegotiateFormat really matches, 406 in your format and Vary: Accept
wrongAnswers: application/json, because q=0 excludes text/csv
An empty string, so the handler should answer 406

cautions: Group middleware does not run for 404 and 405, so typos carry no Sunset.
Cross-origin clients cannot read the headers without Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
A test that fails because v1 still exists after a date is a date bomb.
designGuide.cost: Two DTO sets and their adapters to maintain until the sunset, one middleware, and a route-table test; the real cost is the months of supporting v1 that the headers announce.
strengths: A bug fix in the service reaches both versions at once.
Clients learn the end date and the replacement from standard headers.
One Retirement value keeps headers and tests in agreement.

readings.hint: One header announces a state; the other announces an end.
readings.introduction: A breaking change to a response shape cannot be deployed in place: some clients will keep sending yesterday's requests for months. The route-groups lesson put /v1 and /v2 groups side by side. This lesson adds what makes a second version manageable: a domain type that belongs to neither version, adapters that own each wire shape, standard headers that tell clients when v1 ends, and a route-table test that stops anyone from deleting v1 early.
readings.nuance: Deprecation only discourages the resource and changes no behavior; Sunset is when it may stop responding. The route-table test enforces Sunset, and traffic per route template shows when removal hurts no one.
readings.objective: Serve two API versions from one service through per-version DTO adapters, mark v1 with Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version links, and test that v1 routes survive until the announced date.
readings.question: A v1 group sends Deprecation and Sunset headers and points to /v2 with successor-version links. When is it safe to delete a v1 route registration?
readings.reviewAnswer: After its Sunset date, once its remaining traffic is gone
readings.reviewPrompt: When may a v1 route be deleted?

sections.body: Suppose v1 returned a numeric id, a flat author string and a date, and the product now needs string IDs, a nested author object and a full timestamp. Changing the v1 handler breaks every mobile app that has not updated, and those apps update on their users' schedule, not yours. Copying the whole service into a v2 package fails differently: every bug fix now has to land twice, and the copies drift. The stable middle is one application service and one domain type that know nothing about JSON, plus one small adapter per version that maps the domain value to that version's DTO. A v1 handler and a v2 handler differ only in which adapter they call. Additive changes, such as a new optional field, do not need a new version; reserve /v2 for changes an old client cannot ignore. The compatibility lesson in the Go course covers the other half of the problem, when old and new binaries run during one rollout.
sections.title: Version the wire shape, not the service

sections.body: The program keeps one Notes service and registers both groups on one engine. The v1 group carries a deprecated middleware built from a single Retirement value, which also feeds the route-table check, so the headers and the test can never disagree about the dates. The router receives its clock as a function, so the same engine can be asked what it does today and after the sunset.
sections.title: Two adapters, one service, and a v1 group that announces its end
sections.walkthrough: toV1 and toV2 are the only code that knows either wire shape; handlers fetch a Note and pick an adapter. deprecated computes both header values once: Deprecation is a structured-field date, an at sign followed by Unix seconds, and Sunset is an HTTP-date from http.TimeFormat. Per request it looks up the method and c.FullPath(), the route template, in Successors and fills the v2 template with this request's parameters, so /v1/notes/7 links to /v2/notes/7. Once the injected clock passes the sunset, v1 answers 410 Gone but keeps its links. checkRetirement reads r.Routes(): a v1 route missing before the sunset is a finding, after it the removal is allowed, and every successor must be registered.

sections.body: The three headers answer different client questions. Deprecation (RFC 9745) says the resource is deprecated, or will be, as of a date; it changes nothing about how the request is processed. Sunset (RFC 8594) says when the resource is expected to stop responding, and RFC 9745 adds that the sunset should not be earlier than the deprecation date; a sunset in the past means the resource may vanish at any moment. A Link with rel="successor-version" (RFC 5829) names the replacement, and rel="deprecation" points people at migration notes. Set all of them in group middleware before c.Next, because a header added after the handler has started the body is silently not sent. Know what the middleware cannot reach: Gin's 404 and 405 answers run only engine-level middleware, so a mistyped v1 path carries no Sunset. Browsers hide these headers from cross-origin scripts unless the CORS middleware lists them in Access-Control-Expose-Headers. After the sunset, 410 Gone with the successor link is kinder than 404: it tells a client the path was real and where it went.
sections.title: What Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version promise

sections.body: Adapters run in both directions. A v1 POST body should be decoded into a v1 request DTO and translated into the same domain command v2 uses, so validation and side effects stay in one place. Do not implement v1 by calling the v2 handler and rewriting its JSON: you pay two encodings, and v1 quietly inherits every later v2 change, including ones its clients must not see. Watch for semantic changes that no type shows: if v2 reports durations in milliseconds and v1 in seconds, the conversion belongs in toV1 and in a test. A golden test per adapter, with one captured v1 response checked in as a fixture, catches accidental changes to the old shape when someone edits the domain type. Path versioning, as here, is the easiest scheme to route, cache and label in metrics; with header or media-type versioning, every cache key, log query and dashboard has to learn the header too.
sections.title: Keep version differences inside the adapters

sections.body: checkRetirement takes the time as a parameter. Its own unit tests pin dates on both sides of the sunset, as the program does, so their outcome never changes. The guard on the real router passes time.Now(): until the announced date, deleting a v1 route fails CI, and from the sunset on the same test permits the deletion without anyone editing it. The opposite rule, failing the build because v1 still exists after the sunset, is a date bomb that breaks an unrelated pull request on a calendar day. Track the clean-up with traffic instead: count requests by c.FullPath() as the metrics lesson does, and remove the v1 group when its remaining callers are clients you have contacted, not merely when the date passes.
sections.title: A route-table test that cannot become a date bomb
sections.walkthrough: This fragment belongs in a _test.go file beside newRouter; retirement and seedNotes are the package's own values. The first test guards the real router with the real clock, so it relaxes by itself at the sunset. The second pins both sides of the boundary: an hour before the sunset the deleted list route is exactly one finding, and at the sunset instant, where Before is false, there are none. r.Routes() builds a fresh slice on every call, so DeleteFunc cannot change the engine.

readings.takeaway: Keep the domain version-free and give each version an adapter; put the retirement dates in one value that drives the Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version headers and a route-table test that receives its clock.
readings.title: API versions in Gin: one service under /v1 and /v2, an adapter per version, and a v1 that announces its sunset
wrongAnswers: Once the Deprecation date passes, since it marks the end
As soon as v2 ships, because clients can follow the link

cautions: Catch-all routes have no faithful OpenAPI template.
Only exercised status codes are compared; 4XX and default accept anything in range.
designGuide.cost: About a hundred lines of test helpers and one recording middleware; it checks paths, methods and codes, not body schemas, which need a separate validator.
strengths: Undocumented routes and dead operations fail CI the day they appear.
Status checks reuse the API test table instead of new fixtures.

readings.hint: Compare /v2/notes/7 with the keys of the paths object.
readings.introduction: An OpenAPI document is a promise that clients, generated SDKs and gateway configurations build on, while the router is what actually answers. Nothing connects the two unless you write the check: a handler added on Friday never reaches the document, an operation deleted from code lingers in the SDK, and a handler that starts returning 422 contradicts a spec that says 400. A small test that reads both sides and prints sorted differences keeps them together.
readings.nuance: c.FullPath() returns the template, such as /v2/notes/:id, which maps to /v2/notes/{id}; raw paths would give one key per ID. It is empty for unmatched requests, so the middleware skips NoRoute answers.
readings.objective: Write a test that converts engine.Routes() to OpenAPI path templates, reports routes and operations that exist on only one side, and checks recorded status codes against declared responses.
readings.question: A drift test records the status of each test call and compares it with the OpenAPI responses. Why key the records by c.FullPath() instead of c.Request.URL.Path?
readings.reviewAnswer: It is the route template that matches a spec path key
readings.reviewPrompt: Why record FullPath, not URL path?

sections.body: Drift comes in three shapes, and each hurts a different reader. A route missing from the document is invisible to client generators and API gateways that validate requests against the spec, so the new endpoint works in curl and fails behind the gateway. An operation in the document without a route ships as a method in every generated SDK that returns 404 at runtime. A status code the handler sends but the document does not declare breaks clients that switch on declared responses, and generated clients often treat an undeclared code as a decoding error. None of these fail a build by themselves. It does not matter whether the document is written by hand or generated from annotations: annotations drift from handler code in exactly the same ways, because they are comments that nothing executes. The cure is a test that reads both sides.
sections.title: How a document and a router drift apart

sections.body: The program parses a small OpenAPI 3.1 document, builds a router that disagrees with it in three ways, sends the calls an API test table would send, and prints each finding in sorted order. The document is a string constant only so the example fits in one file; the last section embeds the real file.
sections.title: Diff the route table against the document
sections.walkthrough: operations decodes paths into raw path items and reads only the eight HTTP method keys, because a path item can also hold keys such as parameters and summary. template rewrites each Gin segment: :id becomes {id}, *path becomes {path}, and the catch-all is reported. The observed middleware runs after c.Next, keys each response by method and converted c.FullPath(), and skips requests whose FullPath is empty because they matched no route. drift walks the routes against the operations, then each operation's observed statuses against its declared codes, accepting an exact code, a range such as 4XX or default. Map iteration order never reaches stdout, because only the sorted findings are printed.

sections.body: A Gin :param matches one path segment, which is exactly what an OpenAPI {param} means, so the conversion is mechanical, but the names must match: a document that says /notes/{noteId} for the route /notes/:id produces two findings, and that is correct, because generated clients use the parameter name. A catch-all is different. Gin's *path matches several segments and c.Param returns them with a leading slash, while an OpenAPI path parameter value cannot contain an unescaped slash, so no template describes the route faithfully. Either redesign it, for example as a query parameter, or keep it as a reviewed warning, as the program does. Watch the edges as well: OpenAPI method keys are lowercase, a servers URL such as /api is a prefix the router may or may not include, and the redirects and 405 answers Gin generates are not operations. Gin registers no implicit HEAD or OPTIONS routes, so engine.Routes() holds exactly what your code registered and nothing more.
sections.title: Translate Gin paths into OpenAPI templates

sections.body: Matching routes compares structure; status codes need behavior. The recording middleware observes what the handlers really send, and the natural source of calls is the table the API-tests lesson already runs through the real router, so each success and error case contributes its status for free. The check can only judge codes the table exercises: a 409 that no case triggers is never compared, which is one more reason to give every error kind a row. Use ranges such as 4XX and the default response deliberately, because each one accepts codes nobody reviewed. Requests that match no route have an empty FullPath and Gin's NoRoute answers them, so they are skipped rather than reported against an operation. Checking response bodies against the declared schemas is the next step and needs a JSON Schema validator; the problem-details lesson fixes the error body shape, which keeps that check small.
sections.title: Declared codes against observed codes

sections.body: In the service, embed the document so the binary and the test read the same bytes, and serve those bytes at /openapi.json if clients fetch the spec at runtime. Keep the allow-list of undocumented internal routes in the test file, where every exemption is visible in review. Because the findings are sorted, a CI failure is a stable list that diffs cleanly between runs instead of a different order every time.
sections.title: Run it as a test against the embedded document
sections.walkthrough: This fragment spans two files of the package. spec.go embeds openapi.json into the binary; go:embed patterns are relative to the package directory and cannot contain .., so the document lives beside the package or in a small package of its own that exports the bytes. The test replays the shared case table through a router built with the recording middleware, then reports one error per finding. internal is the reviewed allow-list, including the route that serves the document itself.

readings.takeaway: Treat the OpenAPI document as test input: convert engine.Routes() to templates, fail on routes or operations present on one side only, compare observed status codes with declared responses, and print findings sorted.
readings.title: Keep the OpenAPI document and the Gin router honest: diff routes, operations and status codes in a test
wrongAnswers: URL.Path is empty once Gin has matched a route
FullPath includes the query string the spec declares

cautions: A NoRoute fallback to DefaultServeMux leaks pprof with a 404 status.
pprof.Index only works under the exact /debug/pprof/ prefix.
Secrets passed as flags appear in cmdline and expvar output.
designGuide.cost: A second engine, http.Server and listener with their own budgets and shutdown, plus network policy to keep the port private; profiling itself costs CPU while a profile runs.
strengths: Profiles are available during an incident without a redeploy.
The public router cannot leak diagnostics by construction.

readings.hint: Look at which mux the package's init function writes to.
readings.introduction: A CPU profile or a goroutine dump from a live process can end an incident in minutes, so production services should be able to produce them. The same endpoints in the wrong hands publish the command line, internal function names and memory statistics, and let anyone start a 30-second CPU profile on demand. The safe arrangement is structural: a second Gin engine that serves only diagnostics, hosted by its own http.Server on an address the internet cannot reach.
readings.nuance: Its init calls http.HandleFunc on http.DefaultServeMux, however you import it. Gin never consults that mux, so exposure depends on what serves it: a nil handler, a NoRoute fallback or a second server.
readings.objective: Mount net/http/pprof and expvar on an admin-only Gin engine behind a network and token guard, and prove with httptest that the public engine does not serve them.
readings.question: A Gin service imports net/http/pprof. Which statement about the pprof handlers is true?
readings.reviewAnswer: Registers /debug/pprof/ handlers on DefaultServeMux

sections.body: The package's init function registers five handlers on http.DefaultServeMux: Index for /debug/pprof/ and the named profiles beneath it, Cmdline, Profile, Symbol and Trace, each with a GET method pattern since Go 1.22. expvar's init does the same for GET /debug/vars and publishes two variables, the command line and runtime memory statistics. The registration happens when the package is linked into the binary, whether you import it with a blank identifier or by name to call pprof.Index, and whether the import is in your code or in a dependency. Each endpoint leaks something: cmdline shows every flag, including any secret passed as one; goroutine?debug=2 prints every stack; profile and trace run the CPU profiler or the execution tracer, with their overhead, for as many seconds as the caller asks. A Gin engine never consults the default mux, so it is safe only as long as nothing else serves that mux.
sections.title: What importing net/http/pprof does to the process

sections.body: The program builds both engines and drives them only with httptest recorders, so no port is opened. It first asks the default mux which pattern would serve the debug paths, then shows the public engine's answers, a leaky variant, and the admin engine behind its guard.
sections.title: An admin engine, a guard, and proof that the public engine is clean
sections.walkthrough: http.DefaultServeMux.Handler reports the patterns GET /debug/pprof/ and GET /debug/vars, registered by the init functions of the two imports. The public engine answers every debug path with Gin's plain 404 body. The leaky engine adds NoRoute(gin.WrapH(http.DefaultServeMux)) and serves the whole pprof index, yet its status is still 404: Gin sets 404 before running NoRoute handlers, and the pprof index never calls WriteHeader. adminOnly checks c.RemoteIP() against the allow-list first, then the bearer token with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. gin.WrapF adapts each pprof function, gin.WrapH adapts expvar.Handler(), and the decoded expvar JSON shows the custom counter next to the published command line.

sections.body: The leaky engine is the failure worth remembering. Someone adds a NoRoute fallback to the default mux so a legacy http.Handle registration keeps working, and every debug endpoint becomes public. A test that only checks for status 404 still passes, because Gin preset the status before the wrapped handler wrote its body. Assert the body and Content-Type too, for every path pprof and expvar register, as the program does. The other ways to serve the default mux are just as quiet: http.ListenAndServe(addr, nil), a metrics server built without a handler, or a second http.Server whose Handler field was left empty. If a service needs standard-library handlers next to Gin, give them a private http.NewServeMux and mount that, never the default one. A review rule that rejects a nil handler argument, plus the public 404-body test, closes both paths.
sections.title: A 404 status is not proof

sections.body: pprof.Index chooses a profile by cutting the literal prefix /debug/pprof/ from r.URL.Path. Mount it under /admin/debug/pprof/*any and every profile URL returns the HTML index with status 200, which looks like success and contains no profile. Keep the exact prefix on the admin engine, or wrap the handler in http.StripPrefix and gin.WrapH. In Gin 1.12 the :profile parameter route coexists with the static cmdline, profile, symbol and trace routes, and Gin redirects /debug/pprof to /debug/pprof/ with a 301. Profile and Trace extend the connection's write deadline by the requested seconds through http.ResponseController, which works through Gin because its response writer implements Unwrap. Only one CPU profile can run at a time; a second request gets a 500. The block and mutex profiles stay empty until the program calls runtime.SetBlockProfileRate and runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction.
sections.title: Mount pprof at exactly /debug/pprof/

sections.body: A separate listener is the real boundary; the guard is defense in depth. Bind the admin server to loopback and reach it with kubectl port-forward, or bind it to the Pod address on a port that no public Service or ingress selects and that a NetworkPolicy restricts. The guard uses c.RemoteIP(), not c.ClientIP(), because forwarded headers are client input, as the trusted-proxies lesson explains, and nothing should proxy the admin port anyway. Load the token from configuration rather than a flag, since a flag would appear in the cmdline endpoint it protects, and log every admin request.
sections.title: Two servers in one process
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment; listen is a small helper that calls ListenAndServe and treats http.ErrServerClosed as nil. Each engine gets its own http.Server with its own budgets, and the admin WriteTimeout is a floor that pprof raises per request. errgroup ties the two lifetimes together: if either listener fails, ctx is canceled and both servers shut down within one budget, so the process never keeps serving public traffic with its diagnostics gone, or the reverse.

readings.takeaway: Importing pprof or expvar registers handlers on http.DefaultServeMux; serve them only from a separate, guarded admin engine and listener, and test the public engine for a 404 body, not just a 404 status.
readings.title: Debug endpoints in Gin: pprof and expvar on a separate admin engine and listener, never on the public router
wrongAnswers: Gin's engine serves them at /debug/pprof/ automatically
They are registered only for a blank _ import

cautions: An unknown GIN_MODE panics in Gin init, before main.
With -trimpath the -ldflags value is absent from build info.
ARG and ENV values are readable in the image history.
designGuide.cost: A few build flags and a two-stage Dockerfile; you give up a shell in the runtime image, so debugging moves to logs, the admin listener and ephemeral debug containers.
strengths: /version answers which commit is running in one request.
A static binary on distroless has a tiny attack surface and no shell.

readings.hint: Ask which file the kernel needs before main can run.
readings.introduction: The binary you test with go run is not the one you ship. A release build differs in Gin's mode, in what the toolchain stamps into the executable, in how it links and in the image around it. Each difference has a failure attached: request headers in debug logs, an incident where nobody can say which commit is running, a container that will not start because a C library is missing. This lesson follows the build from the mode switch to the final image.
readings.nuance: With a C compiler present cgo is on, so net and os/user link dynamically and need a loader such as ld-linux. The static image has none, so exec reports no such file or directory; CGO_ENABLED=0 builds a static binary.
readings.objective: Build a Gin service for production with release mode, -trimpath, -ldflags -X and CGO_ENABLED=0, report its identity from runtime/debug build info, and package it in a minimal non-root image.
readings.question: A Gin binary built in the golang image runs on the build host but fails in a distroless static container with "no such file or directory". What is the likely cause?
readings.reviewAnswer: A cgo build needs a C loader the static image lacks

sections.body: Gin reads GIN_MODE once, in its package init, and an empty value means debug, or test under go test. Debug mode prints the route table and warnings to stdout, re-parses templates loaded with LoadHTMLGlob on every render, and when Recovery catches a panic it logs the request's headers with only Authorization masked, so cookies and API-key headers reach the logs. Release mode drops all of that. An unknown value is not ignored: GIN_MODE=production makes SetMode panic inside Gin's init, before main runs and before your logger exists. Pick one owner for the mode. Either the deployment sets GIN_MODE=release and nothing calls SetMode, or validated configuration calls gin.SetMode before any engine is built, as the config-startup lesson does, and GIN_MODE stays unset. Two owners eventually disagree.
sections.title: What Gin's debug mode does in production

sections.body: debug.ReadBuildInfo returns the running binary's own record, which differs on every build, so the program parses a fixed record in the same text format with debug.ParseBuildInfo. It also validates a mode setting, shows what SetMode does with an unknown value, and serves /version twice: as go run links it, and with a version string as -ldflags -X would set it.
sections.title: Report the build identity at /version
sections.walkthrough: ginMode accepts the three names Gin knows and maps an empty setting to release, the opposite of Gin's own default. SetMode panics on anything else, and recover turns that into a printed line here. ParseBuildInfo reads the path, mod, dep and build lines but skips the go line, because ReadBuildInfo fills GoVersion from runtime.Version() separately, so the program sets it by hand. versionFrom prefers the linked string, falls back to the main module version, which go build derives from a VCS tag or reports as (devel), and copies vcs.revision, vcs.time and vcs.modified. Cache-Control: no-store stops caches from reporting a previous deploy's identity.

sections.body: -trimpath removes the build machine's directories from file names recorded in the binary, so stack traces do not reveal home directories and builds from different checkouts match. -ldflags "-X main.version=..." sets a package-level string variable at link time; for other packages it needs the full import path, it works only on a variable that is uninitialized or initialized to a constant string, and a misspelled name is silently ignored, which is why /version should be checked after every build. -s -w drop the symbol table and DWARF data: panics and pprof still name functions because they use the runtime's own tables, but a debugger has less to work with. CGO_ENABLED=0 matters because the golang image has a C compiler, so cgo is on by default and net and os/user link against the system C library.
sections.code:
VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
  go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" -o bin/api ./cmd/api
go version -m bin/api | grep -E 'vcs\.|CGO_ENABLED|trimpath'
file bin/api
sections.title: Build flags that make the binary honest
sections.walkthrough: Run these in your own checkout. git describe prints a tag-based version with a -dirty suffix when the tree has uncommitted changes. go version -m prints the record the /version handler reads; expect vcs.revision, vcs.time, vcs.modified, CGO_ENABLED=0 and -trimpath=true. One surprise: with -trimpath, go build leaves -ldflags out of that record, because linker flags can contain local paths, so the -X value is visible only through the variable it set. file should report a statically linked executable.

sections.body: The containers lesson builds a basic two-stage image on scratch. For a Gin API, the distroless static image is a better default runtime: it adds CA certificates for outbound TLS, time zone data, an /etc/passwd with a nonroot user and a /tmp directory, and still has no shell or package manager. A cgo-linked binary fails in it with a confusing no such file or directory, because the missing file is the dynamic loader, not your program. Use a numeric USER: when a Pod sets runAsNonRoot without a runAsUser, Kubernetes can verify only a numeric image user and refuses to start a container whose image names one. If .dockerignore excludes .git, as it usually should, go build has no VCS data inside the build, the vcs fields are empty and the version is (devel), so CI passes the version in as a build argument.
sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
ARG VERSION=dev
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux go build -trimpath \
    -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" -o /out/api ./cmd/api

# Pin the digest you reviewed: static-debian12:nonroot@sha256:...
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/api /api
USER 65532:65532
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]
sections.title: A multi-stage image with a distroless, non-root runtime
sections.walkthrough: This Dockerfile runs in your own environment: docker build --build-arg VERSION=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty) -t notes-api:dev . The build stage holds the toolchain, module cache and source; only /out/api crosses into the runtime stage. Cache mounts keep downloads and compiled packages between builds without storing them in any layer. The exec-form ENTRYPOINT makes the binary PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM directly, which the rolling-deploys lesson relies on.

sections.body: Anything in a layer or in the image config is readable by everyone who can pull the image, forever. ARG and ENV values are recorded in the image history, so a token passed as a build argument is published; private module credentials belong in a BuildKit secret mount used by a single RUN step and never written to a layer. Environment-specific settings, such as database URLs, tokens, trusted proxy ranges or a debug mode, come from the orchestrator at runtime, so the same digest can be promoted from staging to production as the delivery lesson requires. The source tree, .git, .env files, fixtures and local binaries stay out through .dockerignore. Decide what /version itself may reveal: version, revision, commit time and the modified flag help operators, while hostnames, environment values or the full dependency list help attackers. A production response with modified true is itself a finding: someone shipped uncommitted code.
sections.title: What must not be baked into the image

readings.takeaway: Ship with release mode set by one owner, -trimpath, CGO_ENABLED=0 and a -X version; report vcs.revision, vcs.time and vcs.modified from build info at /version, and run as a numeric non-root user with no secrets in any layer.
readings.title: Shipping a Gin binary: release mode, a /version endpoint from build info, static builds and a non-root image
wrongAnswers: The distroless image has no shell to start the binary
-trimpath removed paths the binary opens at startup

cautions: Delay plus budget must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
Shutdown does not wait for hijacked connections or streams.
A main that returns when ListenAndServe does cuts the drain short.
designGuide.cost: Every Pod termination takes the drain delay plus in-flight time, which lengthens each rollout; the code is one Lifecycle flag, one Drain function and a grace period to keep in sync.
strengths: Rollouts complete without refused connections or cut requests.
An injected clock makes the sequence testable in milliseconds.

readings.hint: Think about who still believes the old Pod is a valid target.
readings.introduction: During a rolling deploy every old replica is told to stop while traffic is still arriving. Calling Shutdown the moment SIGTERM lands closes the listener before every load balancer has heard the replica is leaving, and the requests they still send meet a refused connection. The fix is an ordered sequence with one owner, and because it is about time and ordering, it should be modeled with an injected clock and tested like any other code.
readings.nuance: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM start together, and proxies learn of the removal late. Shutdown closes the listener at once, refusing connections still routed to the Pod; a short serving delay covers that window.
readings.objective: Implement and test a SIGTERM sequence that flips readiness to 503, keeps serving while load balancers stop routing, disables keep-alives, and shuts the http.Server down within a grace period the platform honors.
readings.question: On SIGTERM a Gin service calls http.Server.Shutdown at once, and during rolling deploys some clients see connection refused. Why does a short drain delay before Shutdown fix this?
readings.reviewAnswer: Load balancers still route until endpoint removal spreads

sections.body: When Kubernetes deletes a Pod, two things start in parallel: the control plane removes the Pod's endpoints from its Services, and the kubelet runs any preStop hook and then sends SIGTERM. The endpoint change then has to reach every kube-proxy, ingress controller and cloud load balancer, which takes from milliseconds to several seconds. A process that closes its listener at once refuses connections routed during that window; one that exits drops requests mid-flight; and clients holding keep-alive connections keep reusing the old Pod's sockets. Kubernetes already marks a terminating Pod's endpoints not ready, so for a plain Service the readiness flip mostly confirms what the control plane did. It matters for load balancers and ingress controllers that health-check the Pod directly, and EndpointSlices still publish the probe result as their serving condition. The drain delay is what covers propagation. The server-lifecycle lesson sets the budgets; this one orders the steps.
sections.title: The window where requests get dropped

sections.body: Drain depends only on interfaces: a Clock with After, and the three methods of *http.Server it calls. The model supplies a clock that moves only when told and a server that runs the Gin engine through httptest recorders and refuses requests once Shutdown has closed its listener. main narrates two runs: a slow export that finishes inside the budget, and one that does not.
sections.title: Model the sequence with a fake clock and a fake server
sections.walkthrough: Drain waits for sigterm to close, stores the draining flag that Lifecycle.Readyz reads, disables keep-alives, and only then asks the clock for the delay, so the step message proves the timer exists before main advances. During the delay /readyz answers 503 while /orders is still served, with Connection: close as net/http adds when keep-alives are off. After Advance(5s), Drain registers the budget timer and calls Shutdown; the fake closes its listener, so the next request is refused, and waits for in-flight requests. In the first run the export finishes and Shutdown returns nil. In the second, Advance(20s) fires the budget, the watcher cancels the context and Drain falls back to Close. main prints every line after a channel receive, so scheduling never changes the order.

sections.body: Readiness goes first because it is the only signal some balancers act on; return 503, since Kubernetes HTTP probes count every status from 200 to 399 as success, and keep liveness at 200 throughout, as the metrics-health lesson explains. The delay should exceed a direct health checker's probe period times its failure threshold plus endpoint propagation; five to ten seconds is common, and every Pod in a rollout pays it. SetKeepAlivesEnabled(false) closes idle HTTP/1.1 connections at once and makes each active one close after its current response; HTTP/2 connections get a GOAWAY when their last open stream finishes. Shutdown disables keep-alives too, so the explicit call matters only during the delay, which is the point: clients reconnect while the listener still accepts, and the balancer sends the new connections elsewhere. Shutdown closes listeners and idle connections, then waits for active ones; it does not wait for hijacked connections, and an open Server-Sent Events stream simply holds it until the budget expires, so register a RegisterOnShutdown function that tells streaming handlers to finish.
sections.title: Why the order is readiness, keep-alives, delay, Shutdown

sections.body: Nothing in Drain changes for production. A real clock adapts time.After, *http.Server already has SetKeepAlivesEnabled, Shutdown and Close, and the Lifecycle value is injected into the Gin handler like any other dependency, so the model's tests keep covering the code that ships. The one new obligation is in main, which must not return while the drain is still running.
sections.title: Wire the same Drain to a real signal and server
sections.walkthrough: Run this fragment in your own environment. signal.Stop after the first signal restores default handling, so a second Ctrl-C ends a stuck drain at once. The comment marks the classic bug: ListenAndServe returns http.ErrServerClosed the moment Shutdown begins, and a main that returns then exits with requests still running. If ListenAndServe fails for another reason, such as a port already in use, serve returns that error immediately. Do not derive request contexts from the signal, as the config-startup lesson warns.

sections.body: The grace period countdown starts when the Pod is deleted, before any preStop hook runs, and SIGKILL arrives when it ends, whatever the process is doing. Keep the arithmetic true whenever the delay or budget changes: delay plus Shutdown budget plus the time to close pools and flush telemetry must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds. A preStop sleep is the other place a delay can live, useful when you cannot change the application, but it counts against the same grace period, so never stack it on top of an in-app delay by accident. Pair the sequence with a rollout strategy that keeps capacity, such as maxUnavailable 0 with a surge, as the rollout lesson describes. To verify it in a real cluster, run steady load through kubectl rollout restart and count errors; the target is zero, and the model keeps the ordering from regressing.
sections.code:
# Pod template fragment: merge into a Deployment in your own cluster.
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 35   # delay 5s + Shutdown budget 20s + margin
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/notes-api@sha256:<digest>
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: {path: /readyz, port: 8080}
        periodSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 1
      # Only if the app cannot delay on SIGTERM itself. Distroless images have
      # no shell, so use the sleep action, not exec: ["sleep", "5"].
      # lifecycle:
      #   preStop:
      #     sleep:
      #       seconds: 5
sections.title: Fit the sequence inside the Pod's grace period
sections.walkthrough: Apply this in your own cluster, not in the app. The comment beside terminationGracePeriodSeconds is the budget to recheck on every change. A 2-second probe period with failureThreshold 1 lets anything polling /readyz see the 503 well within the 5-second delay. The commented preStop block is the alternative owner of the delay; the sleep action needs Kubernetes 1.30 or newer, where it is enabled by default, and an exec sleep would fail in an image without a shell.

readings.takeaway: On SIGTERM flip readiness to 503, disable keep-alives and keep serving through a drain delay, then Shutdown within a budget and Close after it; fit delay plus budget inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds and wait for the drain before main returns.
readings.title: Surviving a rolling deploy in Gin: fail readiness, keep serving through a drain delay, then Shutdown
wrongAnswers: Shutdown cancels in-flight requests unless it is delayed
SIGTERM arrives before the replacement Pod has started

lessons.explanation: Gin is a router, a request context and a middleware chain built on top of net/http. A *gin.Engine is an ordinary http.Handler, so everything you know about http.Server, httptest and timeouts still applies. Start with a function that returns a configured engine: main can serve it, and a test can call it directly.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin engine, register routes with a path parameter and exercise them without opening a port.
lessons.title: Your first Gin service: an engine, two routes and a test request

lessons.explanation: Every Gin route is a template stored in a radix tree. The router decides which handler runs, what c.Param returns and whether the client gets a redirect instead of your handler. Most routing bugs are not in handler code: they are a trailing slash, an encoded slash or two templates that cannot share a prefix. Learn the matching rules once and those bugs become predictable.
lessons.objective: Declare Gin route templates with :param and *wildcard, predict how slashes and escapes resolve, and label metrics with c.FullPath().
lessons.title: Path parameters in Gin: :param takes one segment, *wildcard takes the rest, conflicts panic at boot

lessons.explanation: Every query or form value reaches your handler as a string that may be missing, empty, repeated or malformed. Gin offers several helpers that look interchangeable but answer different questions. Choosing the wrong one turns limit=abc into limit 0, or a deliberately empty field into a default the client never asked for.
lessons.objective: Read query and form values with the Gin helper that matches the case, convert them with strconv and reject bad input with a clear 400.
lessons.title: Query strings and forms in Gin: tell absent from empty, parse numbers strictly, bound every limit

lessons.explanation: r.Group("/api/v1") looks like a folder that routes live in, with middleware guarding the door. It is really a registration helper: when you add a route, Gin copies the group's prefix and handler list into that route, and the group plays no part when requests arrive. That one fact explains the most common group bug and tells you how to test for it.
lessons.objective: Organize a Gin API into nested, versioned groups with scoped middleware and prove with r.Routes() that every route has the protection you intended.
lessons.title: Gin route groups: prefixes and middleware are copied at registration, so test the route table

lessons.explanation: The bytes a handler writes are a public contract: field names, which fields exist, how characters are escaped, the Content-Type and the status. Gin has five JSON renderers that look interchangeable and are not, and c.JSON will happily publish every field of whatever struct you hand it, including the ones you add next year.
lessons.objective: Choose between c.JSON, PureJSON, IndentedJSON, SecureJSON and AsciiJSON by their exact output, set status codes deliberately and render a response DTO with correct omitempty and omitzero tags.
lessons.title: Gin JSON responses: know what each renderer writes and return a DTO, never your storage model

lessons.explanation: A single request carries input in four places: path parameters, the query string, headers and the body. Gin has a binder and a struct tag for each, and they compose well as long as you respect two rules the API does not advertise. Every binder validates the entire struct it fills, and a request body can be read only once unless you ask Gin to keep a copy.
lessons.objective: Bind each request source with its own Gin binder and tag, predict what content-type-driven ShouldBind reads, and decode one body twice with ShouldBindBodyWithJSON.
lessons.title: Gin binding sources: bind path, query, headers and body separately, and cache the body to read it twice

lessons.explanation: Gin's binding tags cover shape: required, lengths, ranges, enumerations. Real input also has domain rules, such as a SKU format or an address that is required unless the customer picks the order up. Gin's validator accepts both kinds, but the default error text names Go structs and fields, which makes a poor API. This lesson adds the rules and a response format you can keep stable.
lessons.objective: Register a custom tag and a struct-level rule on Gin's validator, validate slice elements with dive and convert validator errors into a stable field-level JSON response.
lessons.title: Custom validators in Gin: register domain rules once and return field errors clients can rely on

lessons.explanation: Gin middleware is an ordinary handler that happens to run before others in the same chain. Most middleware bugs come from a wrong mental model of that chain: expecting Abort to return, expecting a middleware without c.Next to stop the request, or reading a status before the handler has chosen it. This lesson builds four realistic middleware functions and traces exactly what runs.
lessons.objective: Write Gin middleware that runs code after c.Next, stops the chain with Abort and return, shares typed values through c.Set and c.Get, and is ordered so logs see the final outcome.
lessons.title: Writing Gin middleware: what c.Next returns to, what Abort does not do, and typed request values

lessons.explanation: An upload is attacker-controlled bytes wrapped in attacker-controlled labels. The filename, the declared Content-Type and the size all come from the client, and so does the number of parts. c.FormFile makes accepting a file one line long, which is exactly why the limits, the type decision and the storage name have to be written deliberately around it.
lessons.objective: Accept a multipart upload in Gin with a hard size cap, decide its type from its content, generate the storage name yourself and test it with a request built by mime/multipart.
lessons.title: File uploads in Gin: cap the request, sniff the bytes and never let the client name the file

lessons.explanation: Gin can render server-side HTML with very little code, and Go's html/template does the hardest part, escaping, for you. What Gin leaves to you are the operational decisions: how templates reach the binary, what happens when a template fails halfway, whether a directory listing is exposed and how long browsers and CDNs may keep each file.
lessons.objective: Render html/template pages with c.HTML from templates parsed out of an embedded file system, serve embedded static assets with StaticFS and set cache headers per kind of asset.
lessons.title: Server-rendered HTML in Gin: embed the templates, trust contextual escaping, cache assets on purpose

lessons.explanation: A Gin engine answers misses on its own: a plain-text 404 for unknown paths and, by default, the same 404 for a known path with the wrong method. API clients that expect JSON errors choke on the text, and a 404 for a wrong method sends whoever is debugging in the wrong direction. A few lines of configuration fix both, and the same lesson applies to redirects: the status code decides whether the method and body survive.
lessons.objective: Configure NoRoute, NoMethod and HandleMethodNotAllowed for consistent JSON 404 and 405 responses with a correct Allow header, and choose between 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 for redirects.
lessons.title: 404, 405 and redirects in Gin: answer misses in your own format and pick redirect codes by what must survive

units.summary: Engines, routes, parameters, groups, binding sources, validators, JSON, uploads, templates and 404/405 handling.
units.title: Gin foundations
units.translationNote: Every example runs against upstream Gin v1.12 through httptest in your native development environment. The app's teaching adapter does not promise every Gin API or network-server capability.

lessons.explanation: A Gin engine is an HTTP adapter with a middleware chain. Group prefixes and registration order decide which handlers participate; the framework does not supply your business transaction. Follow one request before introducing authentication, metrics or error middleware. In particular, Abort stops pending handlers but does not return from the current Go function.
lessons.objective: Explain route groups, middleware order and the difference between Abort and return.
lessons.title: Gin routing and middleware: follow the chain and stop it deliberately

lessons.explanation: Binding converts a request into a Go value. It does not prove authorization or a business invariant, and it does not by itself impose your desired body-size budget. A robust handler limits input first, chooses whether errors are returned or immediately written, validates normalized values and only then calls the use case. Return one deliberate response instead of letting several layers compete to write it.
lessons.objective: Reject oversized or invalid input before performing a business side effect.
lessons.title: Gin input: size limits, binding and business validation are separate

lessons.explanation: Gin reuses contexts after a handler returns. Passing the original *gin.Context into a goroutine can observe another request’s mutable state. Copy is useful for limited read-only context access, but it does not extend the response writer’s lifetime, clone every referenced object or give detached work a durable owner. Prefer extracting immutable job input and handing it to a deliberately managed queue.
lessons.objective: Give background work a bounded owner without keeping a pooled Gin context alive.
lessons.title: Gin contexts and goroutines: extract a job, do not retain the response

lessons.explanation: A reverse proxy may supply the original client address, but a direct client can also send X-Forwarded-For. If a Go service trusts forwarding headers from every peer, address-based controls can be bypassed. Configure exactly which proxy origins are trusted and make the edge replace or sanitize incoming forwarding headers. An IP address remains a network observation, not a user credential.
lessons.objective: Configure proxy trust explicitly and keep client IP separate from authentication.
lessons.title: Trusted proxies: forwarded headers are not proof of identity

lessons.explanation: Framework recovery can keep a panic from crashing a request-serving goroutine, but it cannot undo a committed database write or decide whether a remote operation succeeded. Expected application errors should travel through a deliberate mapping policy. Assign one layer to produce the response, and test both its status and public body rather than checking only that the handler returned.
lessons.objective: Test handler contracts through ServeHTTP without confusing recovery with rollback.
lessons.title: Gin errors and tests: one response owner, explicit failure cases

lessons.explanation: A router handles requests, while net/http.Server owns listener behavior and connection budgets. A short r.Run example is useful for a tutorial, but a deployed service needs an explicit startup and shutdown owner. Readiness, request admission, long-lived streams, background workers and shared clients must fit the same lifecycle rather than each inventing its own stop signal.
lessons.objective: Configure native server timeouts and distinguish HTTP drain from worker completion.
lessons.title: Gin in production: the http.Server owns budgets and shutdown

lessons.explanation: Authentication middleware turns an Authorization header into one of two outcomes before any handler runs: a verified principal, or a refusal the client can act on. The bugs live at the edges of that job: a route registered outside the protected group, a MAC compared with ==, a 403 where the client needed a 401, or a debug log that quietly archives every credential it sees.
lessons.objective: Write middleware that verifies an HMAC-signed bearer token, stores a typed principal and answers 401 or 403 for the right reasons.
lessons.title: Bearer authentication in Gin: verify once at the group boundary, hand handlers a typed principal

lessons.explanation: CORS is the protocol a server uses to tell a browser which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it never tightens it. Done carelessly it either breaks a legitimate front end or lets any website read a signed-in user's data. Done correctly it is still not authentication, authorization or CSRF protection, and the server has to keep enforcing those on its own.
lessons.objective: Implement CORS middleware that answers preflights, echoes only allow-listed origins, sets Vary correctly and is never mistaken for access control.
lessons.title: CORS by hand in Gin: an exact origin allow-list, real preflights and Vary: Origin

lessons.explanation: A rate limiter protects shared capacity from one noisy client. Three decisions matter more than the algorithm: what identifies a client, how much memory the limiter may use, and what a refused client is told. Choose the key badly and an attacker gets a fresh bucket on every request. Forget the memory bound and the limiter becomes the leak it was meant to prevent.
lessons.objective: Limit each client with golang.org/x/time/rate, pick a key clients cannot forge, bound the limiter map and refuse with 429 and Retry-After.
lessons.title: Rate limiting in Gin: a token bucket per identity, a bounded map and an honest Retry-After

lessons.explanation: An access log is what you search during an incident. It is only useful if every line carries the same small set of fields, if one request can be followed across services by an ID, and if the log never becomes a second copy of your users' credentials. Gin's built-in Logger prints raw paths with query strings as text, so production services usually replace it with middleware built on log/slog.
lessons.objective: Add request-ID middleware and a structured slog access log that records low-cardinality routes, redacts credentials and can be tested byte for byte.
lessons.title: Request IDs and access logs in Gin: log the route template and the ID, never the credential

lessons.explanation: A request stuck on a slow dependency holds a goroutine, a connection and often a database slot. A deadline bounds that wait, but only if every call below the handler receives the context that carries it. Deadlines are cooperative: Go cannot stop a goroutine from outside, so the safe design lets the handler notice expiry and write the response itself instead of racing it from another goroutine.
lessons.objective: Give each request a deadline that downstream calls inherit, map its expiry to 504, and avoid the timeout patterns that race on the response.
lessons.title: Request deadlines in Gin: one context budget, cooperative handlers, no writes from a second goroutine

lessons.explanation: Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and append small text events to it; the browser's EventSource parses them and reconnects on its own. The protocol is simple, and the engineering is all in the lifecycle. Every event must be flushed through buffers, idle streams need heartbeats, the handler must notice when the client leaves, and the server's write deadline must not cut the stream short.
lessons.objective: Stream SSE from a Gin handler that flushes events, sends heartbeats, ends when the client leaves and survives http.Server's WriteTimeout.
lessons.title: Server-Sent Events in Gin: flush every event, send heartbeats, stop on the request context

lessons.explanation: Health endpoints and request counters are how the platform and the on-call engineer see a service from outside. Each answers a narrow question: should this process be restarted, should it receive traffic right now, and how is each route behaving. Mixing up the first two causes restart storms. Labeling counters with raw paths makes the metrics system the next thing to fall over.
lessons.objective: Separate liveness from readiness, check dependencies within a short budget, and count requests by route template and status class.
lessons.title: Health and metrics in Gin: simple liveness, budgeted readiness, counters keyed by route template

lessons.explanation: A conditional GET lets a client that already holds a copy ask whether it is still current. When it is, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, which saves bandwidth and the client's parsing time. The mechanism has three parts: a validator on every response, a comparison on every request, and a Cache-Control policy that decides who may keep a copy. The policy is where private data leaks.
lessons.objective: Serve ETag and Last-Modified validators, answer conditional requests with 304, and choose Cache-Control so private data never lands in a shared cache.
lessons.title: Conditional GETs in Gin: strong ETags from response bytes, 304 Not Modified and safe Cache-Control

units.summary: Middleware, bounded input, authentication, CORS, rate limits, logging, timeouts, streaming, health, caching and shutdown.
units.title: Gin in production
units.translationNote: Worked upstream Gin examples for your native development environment. The app's teaching adapter does not promise every Gin API or network-server capability.

lessons.explanation: One main.go holding handlers, SQL and business rules works until the first test, the second developer or the second storage backend. This unit grows a single notes API over nine lessons, so this first lesson fixes where each piece lives. Later lessons then add CRUD, pagination, problem details, idempotency and versioning without moving code between packages.
lessons.objective: Organize a Gin API into cmd/api, httpapi, notes and store packages whose imports point toward the domain, with all concrete wiring in main.
lessons.title: Lay out a Gin service so every import points toward the domain

lessons.explanation: A handler that reaches for a package-level database variable works on the first day and fights you afterwards: tests share state, parallel tests race, and no signature tells a reviewer what the handler can touch. Passing dependencies through a constructor makes them visible, replaceable and checked by the compiler. This lesson does that for the notes API, including the clock and the ID source.
lessons.objective: Write handlers as methods on a struct built by a constructor, depend on small consumer-defined interfaces and swap in a fake store for tests.
lessons.title: Give Gin handlers their dependencies through a struct, not globals or context keys

lessons.explanation: CRUD looks like boilerplate until a client depends on the details: whether create tells it where the new note lives, whether PUT without a body field clears it, whether PATCH with false can unpin a note, and whether a duplicate title is a 400 or a 409. This lesson pins down each answer for the notes resource, on top of a mutex-protected in-memory store behind the Store interface.
lessons.objective: Implement create, read, replace, patch and delete for notes with correct status codes, a Location header and presence-aware PATCH fields.
lessons.title: Full CRUD on one resource: exact status codes, a Location header and PUT versus PATCH

lessons.explanation: A GET /notes that returns every row is fine with ten notes and an outage with ten million. Pagination bounds the work per request, but the naive offset version skips or repeats rows when data changes between pages, and a sort parameter pasted into SQL is an injection point. This lesson adds listing, filtering and sorting to the notes API with both failure modes closed.
lessons.objective: Serve stable pages of notes with keyset cursors, cap the page size and accept only allow-listed filter and sort parameters.
lessons.title: Paginate with opaque cursors, a bounded limit and a total order; filter only through allow-lists

lessons.explanation: By now each notes handler writes its own gin.H{"error": ...}. Clients parse several shapes, someone eventually returns err.Error() and leaks a database host, and nobody can list which statuses an endpoint produces. RFC 9457 supplies a standard envelope. A taxonomy in the domain and one mapping function supply the discipline. The errors-testing lesson established one response owner; this lesson gives that owner a contract.
lessons.objective: Return application/problem+json for every failure by mapping a small domain error taxonomy to HTTP statuses in a single Gin middleware.
lessons.title: One error envelope: RFC 9457 problem details mapped from domain errors in one middleware

lessons.explanation: A mobile client sends POST /notes, the connection drops before the 201 arrives, and the client retries. Without help the server creates a second note. HTTP defines PUT and DELETE as idempotent; POST is not, so the client supplies a unique key and the server promises that one key yields at most one effect and one stored response. This lesson adds that promise to the notes API.
lessons.objective: Add Idempotency-Key handling to POST /notes so retries replay the original response, conflicting reuse is rejected and in-flight duplicates wait.
lessons.title: Make POST safe to retry with Idempotency-Key: fingerprint, reserve, replay and expire

lessons.explanation: Two people open the same note. One adds a line; the other fixes the title from the copy loaded earlier, and that second save quietly erases the first edit. Each request was valid on its own. The bug is that the server never asked which version the client was editing. HTTP already has the vocabulary for that question: ETag, If-Match, 412 Precondition Failed and 428 Precondition Required.
lessons.objective: Version the notes resource, expose the version as an ETag and require If-Match on writes so a stale client cannot overwrite a newer edit.
lessons.title: Stop lost updates with versions, ETag and If-Match: 428 when missing, 412 when stale

lessons.explanation: Tests that call a handler function directly miss the bugs that live between handlers: middleware order, error mapping, headers and the exact JSON a client parses. Sending requests through the router production uses, with a fake store behind it, tests the API contract in milliseconds. A table turns the next case into a few lines, and asserting whole bodies is what catches the regression that a status check waves through.
lessons.objective: Write table-driven tests that send requests through the real Gin router with fakes and assert status, contract headers and semantically compared JSON bodies.
lessons.title: Table-driven API tests through the real router: status, headers and JSON compared by meaning

lessons.explanation: The last piece of the notes API is the code that runs first. A typo in an environment variable should stop a deploy with a clear message, not start a server with a default timeout, a debug-mode router or a proxy list that trusts the whole internet. This lesson builds the configuration loader, then assembles every package from the earlier lessons in cmd/api/main.go.
lessons.objective: Load and validate configuration from the environment, fail fast with every problem listed, and wire store, service, handlers, engine and http.Server with signal-driven shutdown.
lessons.title: Start from validated configuration and wire the whole service in one composition root

units.summary: Layout, dependencies, CRUD, pagination, problem details, idempotency keys, optimistic concurrency, API tests and startup.
units.title: Gin project: a complete REST API
units.translationNote: One service grows lesson by lesson. The models run in memory; a deployment adds a database, TLS and observability in your own environment.

lessons.explanation: store.Query(c) compiles because *gin.Context implements context.Context, and in a default Gin engine it quietly throws away cancellation, deadlines and tracing values. The context passed to data access decides whether a query stops when its client leaves and whether background work outlives the response. Gin hands you two candidates, and only one of them is a real request context.
lessons.objective: Predict what *gin.Context returns as a context.Context under each ContextWithFallback setting and give stores and background work a context that is actually canceled, or deliberately not.
lessons.title: *gin.Context is a pooled struct, not your request context: pass c.Request.Context() to stores and goroutines

lessons.explanation: A client that wants to clear a due date sends {"due": null}; a client that only renames a note leaves due out entirely. If the server cannot tell those requests apart, it either ignores the clear or wipes a field nobody mentioned. JSON Merge Patch gives the three cases exact meanings, and Gin's struct binding cannot see one of them.
lessons.objective: Implement an RFC 7396 merge-patch endpoint in Gin that distinguishes absent from null, enforces application/merge-patch+json with 415, and validates the merged result before storing it.
lessons.title: PATCH with JSON Merge Patch in Gin: keep absent, null and value apart, then validate the merged resource

lessons.explanation: List endpoints accumulate filters one release at a time: a status here, a search box there, a second sort key for the dashboard. Each one is a chance to splice a value into SQL text, to let a percent sign widen a search, or to send IN () to the database. Build the query in one function that owns every placeholder, and test that function without a database.
lessons.objective: Write a pure function that turns a Gin list request into SQL text and arguments, with allow-listed sorts, a placeholder for every value, escaped LIKE patterns, bounded IN lists and a unique tiebreaker.
lessons.title: Gin list filters to parameterized SQL: parse strictly, bound IN lists, escape LIKE, end with a tiebreaker

lessons.explanation: A client asks for /posts?include=author,tags so that it can render a feed in one request. The obvious implementation looks up each post's author inside the loop that builds the response, and a page of fifty posts quietly becomes a hundred and one queries. The cost should depend on how many relations were requested, never on how many rows the page holds.
lessons.objective: Serve optional related data on a Gin list endpoint with one batched lookup per relation, bounded concurrent loads and deterministic output, and prove the query count by counting store calls.
lessons.title: ?include= without N+1 in Gin: one batched loader per relation, a bounded errgroup and list-order output

lessons.explanation: A popular public endpoint renders the same page of articles thousands of times a minute, and each render costs a query and a JSON encode. Caching the finished response inside the service removes that work, but only if the cache never answers differently from the handler: not for another user, not for another query string and not after a write.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin middleware that caches public GET responses under a route-template key, never stores per-user responses, coalesces concurrent misses with singleflight and stays correct across writes, TTLs and conditional requests.
lessons.title: Cache public GETs in Gin: key by route template, bypass identity, coalesce misses, invalidate on write

lessons.explanation: A bulk import receives the largest bodies your service will ever see, from clients that may have produced part of the file wrong. Reading it whole turns file size into memory, and one bad row into an unexplained 400. Newline-delimited JSON lets the handler work one record at a time: bound the request, bound each line, judge each row on its own, and tell the client exactly which lines were written.
lessons.objective: Build an NDJSON import endpoint that bounds the body and each line, validates rows one at a time and returns a per-line report whose status matches what was written.
lessons.title: NDJSON imports in Gin: cap the body, decode one bounded line at a time, report each row by its line number

lessons.explanation: An export of a million rows should cost the server one page of rows at a time, not a million rows of memory and a long silence before the first byte. Writing CSV straight into c.Writer and flushing after every page achieves that.
