It also changes the error model: once the first page is on the wire the status line has gone, so a database failure on page forty can no longer become a 500, and the handler needs another way to tell the client the file is incomplete.
lessons.objective: Stream a large CSV from a Gin handler page by page with a safe download filename and formula-safe cells, and make a failure after the first byte visible to the client.
lessons.title: Streaming CSV exports in Gin: keyset pages, two flushes, formula-safe cells and an abort on late failure

lessons.explanation: Some requests ask for work that takes longer than any sensible request budget: a monthly report, a re-index, a large import. Holding the connection open ties up a goroutine, a proxy slot and the client's patience, and a timeout halfway leaves the client unsure whether anything happened. The asynchronous pattern splits the work from the request: the POST validates and enqueues, answers 202 Accepted with the URL of a job resource, and the client polls that resource until it reports a result or a failure.
lessons.objective: Accept slow work with 202 and a job Location, bound it with a queue and a fixed worker pool, refuse overload with 503 and Retry-After, and keep jobs running after the request ends.
lessons.title: Long work behind 202 Accepted in Gin: a bounded queue, fixed workers, a job resource and an honest 503

lessons.explanation: A webhook endpoint is a public URL that anyone can POST to, called by a sender that retries whatever it believes failed. Three things matter more than the business logic: proving the request came from the sender unaltered, refusing old requests replayed by someone who captured one, and processing each event once although it may arrive several times. The status code is an instruction to the sender's retry machinery, so choose it as carefully as the verification.
lessons.objective: Receive signed webhooks in Gin by authenticating the raw body before binding, rejecting replays, deduplicating deliveries and choosing status codes that make the sender retry only when a retry can help.
lessons.title: Signed webhooks in Gin: verify the raw bytes, reject stale timestamps, dedupe event IDs, answer fast

units.summary: Request contexts, JSON Merge Patch, safe filters, batched includes, response caches, streaming import and export, async jobs and signed webhooks.
units.title: Gin and your data
units.translationNote: Stores are in-memory models driven through httptest. Point the same handlers at your own isolated database in a native development environment.

lessons.explanation: Most Gin services are also HTTP clients: they call a payment provider, an inventory service or a search cluster while their own caller waits. Every such call borrows the caller's time, a pooled connection and memory for the reply. Done naively, one slow or misbehaving upstream turns into piled-up goroutines, exhausted sockets and error responses that quote another team's database errors to your users.
lessons.objective: Call an upstream HTTP API from a Gin handler through a shared, budgeted http.Client and map every failure to your own 404, 502 or 504 without leaking upstream details.
lessons.title: Upstream calls from Gin: one shared client, the request deadline, a bounded body and your own error codes

lessons.explanation: A retry turns a transient failure into a success and a persistent failure into extra load at the worst possible moment. Whether a retry helps depends on three questions: is it safe to send the request twice, is the failure likely to clear soon, and how much extra traffic is the fleet already sending. This lesson builds the client side of those answers behind a Gin handler, with a seeded random source and an injected clock so every wait is reproducible.
lessons.objective: Wrap upstream calls in a retry policy that respects idempotency, Retry-After and a shared budget, and use a circuit breaker so Gin answers 503 quickly while a dependency is down.
lessons.title: Retrying upstream calls from Gin: only when safe, jittered backoff, a retry budget and a circuit breaker

lessons.explanation: JSON, CSV and HTML often shrink several times under gzip, which matters on mobile links and metered egress. A compression middleware sits between every handler and the network, so its bugs appear everywhere at once: a missing Vary header serves gzip to a client that cannot read it, a stale Content-Length truncates bodies, a compressed event stream stalls, and a page that mixes a secret with reflected input becomes a BREACH oracle.
lessons.objective: Write a gzip middleware for Gin that negotiates Accept-Encoding correctly and skips responses that must not be compressed, and accept gzip request bodies without a decompression-bomb hole.
lessons.title: Gzip in Gin by hand: negotiate q-values, wrap the writer, add Vary and know what never to compress

lessons.explanation: A download endpoint looks like one line, c.File(path), and that line hides most of the behavior: byte ranges for resumed and parallel downloads, conditional requests, HEAD, the content type and the filename the browser saves. Knowing what Gin delegates to net/http and what it adds decides whether a large export resumes after a dropped connection or starts over, and whether a user-chosen filename can break the response header.
lessons.objective: Serve downloadable files from Gin with correct Range, If-Range, ETag and HEAD behavior, a Content-Disposition built by mime.FormatMediaType and file access confined to an os.Root.
lessons.title: File downloads in Gin: ServeContent for ranges and validators, a safe Content-Disposition, files opened by ID

lessons.explanation: Content negotiation lets one URL return the representation each client prefers: JSON for an API client, CSV for a spreadsheet import, HTML for a browser. Gin offers c.NegotiateFormat and c.Negotiate for this, and reading their v1.12.0 source shows that they implement much less of the HTTP rules than their names suggest. The gaps are easy to close, but only once you know where they are.
lessons.objective: Serve JSON, CSV and HTML from one Gin handler with q-value-aware negotiation, a 406 that lists what is available, Vary: Accept for caches and a ?format= override where URLs must name the representation.
lessons.title: Content negotiation in Gin: what NegotiateFormat really matches, 406 in your format and Vary: Accept

lessons.explanation: A breaking change to a response shape cannot be deployed in place: some clients will keep sending yesterday's requests for months. The route-groups lesson put /v1 and /v2 groups side by side. This lesson adds what makes a second version manageable: a domain type that belongs to neither version, adapters that own each wire shape, standard headers that tell clients when v1 ends, and a route-table test that stops anyone from deleting v1 early.
lessons.objective: Serve two API versions from one service through per-version DTO adapters, mark v1 with Deprecation, Sunset and successor-version links, and test that v1 routes survive until the announced date.
lessons.title: API versions in Gin: one service under /v1 and /v2, an adapter per version, and a v1 that announces its sunset

lessons.explanation: An OpenAPI document is a promise that clients, generated SDKs and gateway configurations build on, while the router is what actually answers. Nothing connects the two unless you write the check: a handler added on Friday never reaches the document, an operation deleted from code lingers in the SDK, and a handler that starts returning 422 contradicts a spec that says 400. A small test that reads both sides and prints sorted differences keeps them together.
lessons.objective: Write a test that converts engine.Routes() to OpenAPI path templates, reports routes and operations that exist on only one side, and checks recorded status codes against declared responses.
lessons.title: Keep the OpenAPI document and the Gin router honest: diff routes, operations and status codes in a test

lessons.explanation: A CPU profile or a goroutine dump from a live process can end an incident in minutes, so production services should be able to produce them. The same endpoints in the wrong hands publish the command line, internal function names and memory statistics, and let anyone start a 30-second CPU profile on demand. The safe arrangement is structural: a second Gin engine that serves only diagnostics, hosted by its own http.Server on an address the internet cannot reach.
lessons.objective: Mount net/http/pprof and expvar on an admin-only Gin engine behind a network and token guard, and prove with httptest that the public engine does not serve them.
lessons.title: Debug endpoints in Gin: pprof and expvar on a separate admin engine and listener, never on the public router

lessons.explanation: The binary you test with go run is not the one you ship. A release build differs in Gin's mode, in what the toolchain stamps into the executable, in how it links and in the image around it. Each difference has a failure attached: request headers in debug logs, an incident where nobody can say which commit is running, a container that will not start because a C library is missing. This lesson follows the build from the mode switch to the final image.
lessons.objective: Build a Gin service for production with release mode, -trimpath, -ldflags -X and CGO_ENABLED=0, report its identity from runtime/debug build info, and package it in a minimal non-root image.
lessons.title: Shipping a Gin binary: release mode, a /version endpoint from build info, static builds and a non-root image

lessons.explanation: During a rolling deploy every old replica is told to stop while traffic is still arriving. Calling Shutdown the moment SIGTERM lands closes the listener before every load balancer has heard the replica is leaving, and the requests they still send meet a refused connection. The fix is an ordered sequence with one owner, and because it is about time and ordering, it should be modeled with an injected clock and tested like any other code.
lessons.objective: Implement and test a SIGTERM sequence that flips readiness to 503, keeps serving while load balancers stop routing, disables keep-alives, and shuts the http.Server down within a grace period the platform honors.
lessons.title: Surviving a rolling deploy in Gin: fail readiness, keep serving through a drain delay, then Shutdown

units.summary: Upstream clients, retries and circuit breakers, compression, ranged downloads, content negotiation, versioning, contract tests, admin endpoints, release builds and rolling deploys.
units.title: Gin in the wider system
units.translationNote: Upstreams, listeners and signals are modeled in-process. Real deployments, load balancers and clusters belong to your own environment.
